#2104. Arsenal Confirm 19 Players on November International Duty

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

There is no breathing space for the Arsenal squad. 19 players are going to represent their countries in international fixtures in the final break of 2026. Many will face crucial moments in the coming days with Nations League promotions and relegations still at stake.

There are plenty of important fixtures in November. A number of Arsenal players will be looking to help their countries qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals. However, whilst others will be battling to avoid relegation. A number of Gunners will also be facing their club teammates in some interesting fixtures.

One of the biggest matches will be the clash between England and Spain on November 15th in Madrid.

Spain includes David Raya, Martin Zubimendi and Mikel Merino in their squad, meaning they could face five Arsenal teammates. Declan Rice, Eberechi Eze, Ben White, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Ezri Konsa are all in Thomas Tuchel’s England squad.

Spain lead England by three points in their Nations League group, but the Lionesses have a chance to keep their quarter-final hopes alive if they can defeat Croatia at Wembley on November 12.

Konsa will be absent during the first match as he undertakes personal training, but he could return in time for the encounter against Spain.

There is more Arsenal interest in Group A2. Jurrien Timber’s Netherlands facing Christos Tzolis’ Greece on November 13, followed by a clash with Kai Havertz’s Germany three days later.

Both the Netherlands and Greece are tied on eight points. Germany will be looking to move up in the standings against Serbia.

These games could affect how a number of Arsenal players come back into the fold with such a busy run of fixtures.

Viktor Gyokeres has the chance to help Sweden move up to League A.

The forward has scored four goals in four Nations League games. Sweden are two points clear at the top of their group. A win against Bosnia and Herzegovina on November 14 will guarantee them a promotion.

They then head to Poland for their final game. Gyokeres will be looking to continue his goal scoring and return to Arsenal with confidence.

However, Martin Odegaard will have a tough task ahead. Norway currently sit bottom of their group having only picked up three points from four games.

With three points behind second place Denmark, Norway will host Wales before heading to Denmark on November 17. Both games will be crucial for the Norwegians to avoid relegation.

Riccardo Calafiori will be on duty for Italy against France and Belgium. Piero Hincapie has two friendly matches against Ecuador, one against Costa Rica and one against Bolivia.

Bruno Guimaraes and Gabriel Magalhaes will be travelling to play against Japan and Singapore with Brazil. Kepa Arrizabalaga has received his first call-up to the Basque squad for their friendly against Venezuela.

James Scanlon could have a successful campaign with Gibraltar. Two wins against Andorra and Malta would see them top their group and progress to League C.

With so many Arsenal players playing in competitive matches, the international break could have an impact on a number of countries. Mikel Arteta will be hoping his players return in good condition before they resume their domestic campaign.

#2103. Chelsea news: Stewart departure, Scott interest and Bournemouth preparations

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. Chelsea’s sporting department is facing another change following news of Laurence Stewart’s impending departure, while the club continue to be linked with potential additions to their squad.

Alex Scott and Palmeiras teenager Eduardo Conceicao have both featured in Thursday’s transfer coverage, with Xabi Alonso also preparing his players for Saturday’s Premier League meeting with Bournemouth.

Here is our 7pm round-up of the latest Chelsea news for Thursday, 8 October.

Laurence Stewart is set to leave Chelsea by mutual consent after almost four years at Stamford Bridge, with the club planning to redistribute his responsibilities rather than appoint a direct replacement.

His departure is understood to be amicable and will not take immediate effect. Stewart joined from Monaco in 2022, initially as technical director, before becoming co-sporting director alongside Paul Winstanley.

As detailed in our report on Stewart’s departure and Chelsea’s leadership reshuffle, Winstanley, Sam Jewell and Joe Shields are expected to take on expanded responsibilities across recruitment, player development and the wider BlueCo operation.

The changes follow discussions about the club’s sporting structure that reportedly began earlier this year. There is no confirmed suggestion that Stewart’s departure resulted from a disagreement with Alonso.

Chelsea’s reported interest in Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott remains a talking point, despite the south coast club’s determination to retain the England international.

The Blues reportedly had a £64m offer rejected during the summer, with Matt Law of The Telegraph subsequently identifying Chelsea as leading contenders for the 23-year-old.

However, as examined in our latest report on Chelsea’s interest in Scott, Bournemouth are not expected to entertain a January sale.

Scott’s immediate concern is recovering from a thigh injury suffered while representing England. The midfielder could face several weeks on the sidelines, potentially complicating Bournemouth’s plans as well as any future discussions about his next move.

Chelsea have also reportedly made contact with Palmeiras over 16-year-old forward Eduardo Conceicao, who is attracting attention from several leading European clubs.

According to Mark Brus of CaughtOffside, Chelsea have held discussions with the Brazilian club as they explore the possibility of a future deal.

Our report on Chelsea’s interest in Eduardo Conceicao explains that a valuation as high as €100m has been suggested, although that figure is not a confirmed asking price or evidence of a formal bid.

Manchester City, Arsenal and Real Madrid are among the other clubs reportedly monitoring the teenager. Conceicao would be unable to complete a transfer to England until he turns 18, making any prospective move a longer-term consideration.

Alonso’s attention will now turn to Saturday’s Premier League meeting with Bournemouth at Stamford Bridge.

The match kicks off at 3pm and will not be televised live in the United Kingdom because of the Saturday afternoon broadcasting blackout.

Our Chelsea v Bournemouth kick-off and how-to-watch guide provides the full details, including how to follow the match and the available overseas broadcast information.

Scott’s injury is expected to deprive Bournemouth of an important midfield option, although Chelsea will have their own fitness decisions to make as players return from international duty.

After Saturday’s fixture, Chelsea travel to Hill Dickinson Stadium to face Everton on 17 October. Alonso will be looking for greater consistency as the domestic programme resumes.

#2102. Arsenal youngster suffers international injury setback

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Ceadach O’Neill has suffered a setback in his development after being ruled out of the Northern Ireland squad due to injury.

O’Neill had been named by Michael O’Neill in the squad for the last two games of the Nations League against Ukraine and Hungary. The 18-year-old was hoping to make his first senior start after appearing in four games for Northern Ireland, but all as a substitute.

However, he will miss the international break after suffering an injury. He was also unable to play in Arsenal’s Under-21s 5-2 win over Aston Villa on Sunday.

The news comes at a good time for the winger who has recently been getting more attention in Arsenal’s first team.

O’Neill has impressed Mikel Arteta in training with the senior players and has also made his first team debut in the Carabao Cup.

His performances have indicated he may be another academy player who will fight for a spot under Arteta. He also impressed during Arsenal’s loss to Fleetwood in the Carabao Cup.

The teenager was one of only a few players to leave the game with their head held high after providing Gyokeres with a good cross to bring the score back level.

He was also included in the Arsenal squad that travelled to Liverpool in the Premier League. Although he did not play, it was still a positive result.

The inclusion of the Northern Ireland call-up means he could continue to develop. Getting his first senior start would help him show he can perform outside of the academy.

O’Neill’s departure is a key moment for Northern Ireland. They still have much to play for in their final Nations League fixtures.

The squad sit one point above Hungary in Group B2 with Ukraine four points behind. They must now face Ukraine before they take on Hungary.

A first-place finish would guarantee promotion to League A. Finishing second would see them enter the promotion play-offs. With a promising young player leaving after the last international break, Michael O’Neill will be disappointed to lose him.

The manager praised O’Neill for his contribution to the squad and wished him a speedy recovery. The winger will now work on getting back to full fitness.

His recent inclusion in the first team, shows how far he has come in recent weeks. He will be hoping to get another chance when he is fully fit.

#2101. Arsenal could use Berta connection to explore Endrick transfer

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal may be able to pursue a January move for Endrick. Andrea Berta providing a useful contact for the forward’s representatives.

A move to the Premier League is being linked with the young Real Madrid player after he failed to play regularly for his current Spanish club. As such, his representatives want to find a new club for him in the winter window.

With Bukayo Saka injured, Arsenal may be looking to strengthen their attacking options. Endrick’s ability to play in central areas and wide areas can make him an attractive option for Mikel Arteta.

But it’s not that simple. The North Londoners are not currently amongst the clubs who are pushing hardest to sign the Brazilian.

The TalkSPORT report that Berta’s links to Endrick’s representatives could provide Arsenal with an ideal starting point if they wish to pursue a deal.

The forward has been offered to a number of clubs in the Premier League as his camp seek to resolve his lack of opportunities in Real Madrid.

Arsenal are known to have been interested in the forward in the past. Newcastle United, Aston Villa and Tottenham are the clubs currently gaining more concrete attention.

It doesn’t mean they can’t make a move to north London. Berta’s connections may help them understand what is needed to get the player to the Emirates.

However, Real Madrid may be more reluctant to let the player go. The Spanish club have been reluctant to allow Endrick to leave before, making a loan look more of a realistic option.

Endrick arrived at Real Madrid with an incredible reputation having made his breakthrough at Palmeiras. However, due to there being competition for places, he has struggled to play much in Spain.

If he were to go to the Premier League, he would be able to play regularly to help his development. Playing under Arteta and competing for major trophies at Arsenal would be a great opportunity.

However, Arsenal would have to consider whether he would actually play enough. Moving to another team with competition for attacking spots may not be the best move for his development.

Arsenal need to decide whether Endrick would fill a real gap in their attacking line-up or simply add to their talented front line.

Although Saka’s injury makes attacking additions more important, they can’t make a decision based purely on the injury. They need to look at how he would fit into their future plans.

Thanks to Berta’s link, Arsenal can look into the possibility of signing him. Whether he is a serious target will depend on Real Madrid’s willingness to let him go and what Arsenal can offer him.

#2100. Transfer insider outlines Liverpool’s stance on selling Frimpong amid reported Saudi interest

Liverpool could potentially be open to selling Jeremie Frimpong for the right price in 2027, according to one transfer insider.

The Dutchman joined the Reds from Bayer Leverkusen almost 18 months ago and scored on his debut in the Community Shield, but unfortunately his time at Anfield so far has been dogged by several injury absences.

The 25-year-old has been sidelined with a muscle problem he incurred in the victory at Brentford last month, when he was forced off just seven minutes after his introduction as a half-time substitute, whilst he’s also shipped criticism over the nature of some of his performances this term.

According to Pete O’Rourke for Football Insider, Liverpool could ‘consider’ selling Frimpong next year, and the right-back has reportedly been attracting transfer interest from Saudi Pro League outfit Al-Hilal.

The Merseysiders won’t sanction a January exit for the Netherlands international due to concerns over squad depth amid the ongoing long-term absence of Conor Bradley, but club and player could be open to a summer departure if a ‘big offer’ is tabled.

The transfer insider also claimed that Andoni Iraola doesn’t have the strength in depth that he’d like, with the Basque feeling that his squad is lighter than many of the Reds’ direct rivals.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

First things first, there’s no way that Liverpool are in a position to consider offloading Frimpong in January, even if Bradley manages to return by then.

The latter will take time to fully get up to speed after not playing for nearly a whole year, and his own injury history isn’t the most auspicious either.

Ronald Araujo is currently doing an excellent job at right-back, but it isn’t his natural position and it remains to be seen whether or not his loan move from Barcelona will be converted into a permanent transfer.

If that does happen and Bradley rediscovers the strong performance levels that he’d shown prior to his knee injury, maybe then Liverpool would have more scope to consider a substantial offer for Frimpong if he’s not getting much of a look-in under Iraola.

For now, though, the Dutchman is very much needed at Anfield, and hopefully he’ll become available for action once the November international break has concluded towards the end of next week.

#2099. Arsenal receive positive Piero Hincapie injury update ahead of return

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Piero Hincapie has provided some good news for an Arsenal team that have struggled at the start of the season by confirming that he is now fully fit.

The defender has had two separate injury issues since joining Mikel Arteta’s squad but feels he is now over the setbacks and ready to play regularly.

Hincapie is playing for Ecuador in their November international fixtures. His inclusion in the squad was also a positive, as he was unable to play in their last camp due to injury.

Hincapie initially missed Ecuador’s September squad because of a groin problem. He had been named among the substitutes for Arsenal’s final match before that break, against Brighton.

After recovering, the 24-year-old returned to action in the 2-1 Premier League win over Leeds United on October 10. However, he suffered another setback during the warm-down after the match.

The ankle injury was particularly unfortunate, with Hincapie having to leave the pitch with assistance from goalkeeper Illan Meslier. He subsequently missed Arsenal’s matches against Lille and Nottingham Forest.

Mikel Arteta had at first suggested that Hincapie could be out for a matter of weeks, but the defender has since rejoined individual training.

He has now given a much more positive update on his injury whilst on international duty. He is now “100% fit” and does not have any niggles.

This is great news for Arteta. He has had to be cautious with his defensive choices throughout the campaign.

Hincapie will have a chance to get some much-needed game time while he is included in the squad to play Ecuador.

He has been included in the squad by Marcelo Gallardo to face Costa Rica (13th November) and Bolivia (17th November) in friendly games. This will be the first games Ecuador play at home under their new head coach.

Hincapie has also expressed his optimism for his initial discussions with Gallardo. The player is excited to work under the former River Plate manager and help the national team.

He should prove to be a valuable asset in the squad, considering he can play in both roles. He is a natural centre back but can also play as a left back.

Hincapie has shown that he is happy to play anywhere in the team his manager requires. This can be an important factor for Arsenal as the fixture list gets tougher.

He has only featured three times in all competitions this season and has yet to play in the Premier League. Consistent playing time will be key if he is to become a regular in Arteta’s plans.

However, his latest update shows that he is no longer struggling with the physical issues. If he can stay fit over the international break, he will provide another key defensive option for Arsenal in the coming weeks.

#2098. Arsenal receive mixed verdict after Liverpool penalty review

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

We’ve an important update on the Arsenal Liverpool penalty decision. Arsenal received a mixed reaction from the Premier League’s independent panel after their controversial win at Anfield.

The panel were unanimous in their decision that Liverpool should have been awarded a penalty after Jurrien Timber tugged Alexander Isak’s shirt. However, they were divided on whether it should have been reviewed by VAR.

The panel also cleared the officials on the incident involving Noni Madueke. This means that Arsenal were justified in their win due to the wrong decision being made on the penalty.

The incident happened during the 1-0 win for Arsenal at Anfield on November 1. Isak was trying to run onto a cross from Bradley Barcola after Kai Havertz had given the Gunners the lead.

As Timber pulled him back, he was unable to cleanly head the ball. The referee Andy Madley allowed play to continue. The decision was then made by VAR Stuart Attwell that there was not enough evidence to suggest a review.

The five-man Key Match Incidents panel has now ruled that this was the wrong decision. Four of the panel voted that Liverpool should have been awarded the spot kick after Timber’s handball.

However, there was a tight vote on whether VAR should have intervened. Three panellists felt that Attwell should have shown Madley to the pitchside monitor, whilst two felt it did not reach the threshold.

One panellist felt the length of the hold was not long enough to affect the movement of Isak. The other two members who felt that VAR should not have intervened also said that it is subjective as to how much the hold would affect the striker.

This is an important point to note. Whilst they agreed that the penalty was deserved, there was less agreement on whether it was VAR’s responsibility to overturn the decision.

There was also good news for Arsenal in the panel’s decision regarding Madueke’s late altercation with Alexis MacAllister.

The Liverpool midfielder fell to the floor following a headbutt from the Arsenal winger. The incident was reviewed by the VAR, but Madueke was spared a red card. Mac Allister received a yellow.

All five panel members agreed that Madueke should not have been sent off. They felt that there had not been any contact, and Mac Allister’s reaction was certainly excessive.

It certainly gives us an alternative standpoint into the situation. Whilst Arsenal benefited from the incorrect decision regarding the penalty, the officials were backed up with the disciplinary incident.

This won’t have any impact on the result of the Anfield game, as Havertz’s goal was the winning goal and gave Arsenal their first league victory at the stadium in 14 years.

However, it does show how risky Timber was to make the challenge and how close the panel were with whether they should have intervened with VAR.

#2096. Arsenal face January dilemma as Liverpool and Chelsea join Alex Scott transfer race

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal have made contact with Bournemouth over a potential move for Alex Scott. Mikel Arteta may have to rethink his transfer plans if competition for the midfielder intensifies.

According to The i Paper, Arsenal, Liverpool and Chelsea have all made exploratory enquiries about the 23-year-old. The clubs want to establish what it would take to persuade Bournemouth to sell. However, none appears close to agreeing to a deal.

Arsenal are believed to be keen on a summer move. Liverpool and Chelsea are more interested in signing Scott in January. However, if they were to make a serious offer, it could be hard to hold out.

Scott has become one of the most exciting midfielders in the Premier League. He is an attractive option for clubs looking to improve their squad going forward due to his age, experience and being a homegrown player.

However, there is some uncertainty around Scott’s future. The England international has turned down two contract offers and is unwilling to sign a new deal. There are 18 months left on Scott’s contract, meaning it is an increasingly important decision for Bournemouth.

Arsenal are interested in Scott with doubts surrounding their own midfield options. There have been reports linking Martin Zubimendi and Mikel Merino to exits.

Scott would give Arteta another option, but Arsenal will have to consider if they want to make a move and give Liverpool and Chelsea an advantage.

Bournemouth are reported to want more than £100m to let him go during the January transfer window.

It would be a big asking price, especially given that Scott has 18 months left on his contract. There are a few reasons why Bournemouth could be holding out for a big fee.

The Cherries had to pay £25m to bring Scott in from Bristol City, who will receive 20 per cent of any future transfer fee. They will also have to find a suitable replacement at the halfway stage.

Reports said Chelsea received a number of offers worth around £70m in the summer, but Bournemouth have rejected claims that a bid of £80m will get them talking.

Scott is believed to be happy to stay at the club until the end of the campaign. Bournemouth are also having a great season under Marco Rose, currently sitting in seventh place in the Premier League with eight straight wins in all competitions.

Arsenal have little to hurry into any deal and could use the summer to negotiate a better deal. This is especially true with Scott’s contract situation becoming more of an issue.

The problem is that Liverpool and Chelsea are keen competitors and could lead to a bidding war in January, leaving Arsenal with little room to negotiate.

Whilst Arsenal have made their interest known, this doesn’t necessarily mean he will be moving anytime soon. If Scott is a genuine target, then they must be prepared to pounce if the situation arises.

#2094. Viktor Gyökeres makes Arsenal future clear as striker responds to exit speculation

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Viktor Gyökeres has put to bed any doubts over his future at Arsenal by stating his desire to stay.

The striker has been under question over his long-term future under Mikel Arteta after a difficult start to the 2026/27 season. His latest comments suggest he will not be seeking a move away from north London.

Gyökeres moved to Arsenal for £63.5m from Sporting Lisbon last summer. He’s played a key role in the club winning the Premier League last season with 14 league goals.

However, he has not featured as much this season. Kai Havertz often being Arteta’s go-to man centrally, resulting in him only starting once in the Premier League.

This has led to some speculation that the Sweden international may look at his options in January. However, his latest interview with the Swedish outlet Fotbollskanalen suggests otherwise.

Gyökeres was asked if he wants to stay at Arsenal and has made it clear he wants to continue his career at the Emirates.

The striker also spoke about his relationship with Arteta.

He explained that they regularly discuss football, the team’s approach and the opposition. Those conversations also help him understand what Arteta expects when he is selected to start.

It is a key point to note that just because he hasn’t had much time on the pitch doesn’t mean there have been any issues between the two.

Gyökeres has begun to show his worth again in recent weeks. He found the net against Fleetwood in the League Cup and then Slavia Prague in the Champions League.

This came after a long time to get his first goal of the season and gives him the chance to remind Arteta what he can bring to the team.

There is no doubt that Gyökeres has not lived up to the expectations he had when he came from Portugal.

But his overall effect cannot be ignored. He has contributed 23 goals and 6 assists in 69 games for Arsenal.

The challenge will be finding a way to get the best out of him and Havertz. They add different attributes, and Arteta will have plenty of options to choose from depending on the opposition.

They will also want to avoid losing someone they have invested heavily in so early on. Gyökeres has a contract until 2030, so they are in a great position.

His latest comments will help to reassure fans that he is not looking to leave the club after stating his ambition to play more games and make himself an indispensable part of Arteta’s squad.

The main thing for Arsenal will be to make sure that he can turn this attitude into consistent performances. Gyökeres has made his intentions clear and now needs to show why they brought him to North London in the first place.

#2092. Newcastle kit fiasco sums up haphazard pre-season

Newcastle’s pre-season friendly against Bayer Leverkusen at St James’ Park took a bizarre turn when a kit clash prompted the hosts to change shirts midway through the first half.

The German team’s white away kit with blue trim proved hard to distinguish from Newcastle’s home strip, which has a white back and blue stripes across the shoulders.

During the first-half hydration break, Newcastle decided to change into their lilac third kit, which improved the viewing experience for fans who took to social media to question the original choice of kits.

Newcastle would go on to lose the game 2-1 in new manager Matthias Jaissle’s first game at St James’, a result which followed a 3-1 reverse against Everton on Wednesday evening.

Leverkusen, the 2023-24 Bundesliga champions now managed by Spaniard Carles Martínez Novell, scored after just 44 seconds through a powerful Ibrahim Maza strike.

Jaissle’s team found their feet as the first 45 minutes progressed, with Yoane Wissa their biggest attacking threat. The striker endured a difficult first season at the club, but his performances at the World Cup with DR Congo appear to have restored confidence.

Newcastle were level just before half-time, when Malick Thiaw rose highest to plant home a back-post header from a corner. Former Brentford goalkeeper Mark Flekken appealed in vain for a foul, but there was no infringement.

After changing all 10 outfield players at half-time against Everton, Jaissle was more circumspect with second-half substitutes; Rory Finneran for Lewis Miley was the only change before the 80th minute.

Newcastle faded though, and the game was won by Victor Boniface scoring just a few minutes after coming on as a substitute. The Nigeria striker wrong-footed Sean Steur with an impudent piece of skill before rolling the ball into the bottom corner.

The North-East club are coming to terms with the departures of Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães this summer, as well as manager Eddie Howe. They have one more pre-season friendly to play, against Strasbourg on Sunday, before they begin their Premier League campaign at home to Liverpool.

Newcastle United (4-2-3-1) Hornicek; M Miley (Pivas 81), Thiaw, Botman, Hall; Steur, L Miley (Finneran h-t); Elanga, Woltemade (Neave 86), Barnes; Wissa. Subs Charlton, Harris (g), Sanusi, Johnson.

Bayer Leverkusen (4-2-3-1) Flekken; Vazquez (Tape h-t), Bade, Tapsoba, Gutierrez (Belocian 70); Garcia, Fernandez (Terrier 70); Maza (Boniface 80), Tillman (Doganay 70), Moreira (Tella 80); Kofane (Schick h-t). Subs Hofmann, Arthur, Oermann, Poku, Blaswich (g), Alfa-Ruprecht, Hawighorst, Lomb (g).

Referee Michael Oliver (Durham). Attendance 39,059

A second pre-season defeat in a week for Newcastle. Just like against Everton, they faded in the second 45 minutes but Jaissle decided to leave some tired legs out there for fitness purposes. The performances of Barnes and Wissa were promising, but Newcaslte are giving up chances.

Newcastle had a free-kick with the last kick of the game, but Harvey Barnes loops the delivery straight into Flekken’s gloves.

Schik with a chance to wrap up the victory, but Hornicek saves before Thiaw clears to deny Terrier a tap in on the rebounds.

There will be just three minutes of added time to play.

Elanga fouled near the touchline, but time is running out. The free-kick won by Neave came to nothing.

Chance for Barnes! Good combination play involving Elanga and Wissa down the right, and the ball flashed across the six-yard box. Barnes almost steered it in, but did not make firm enough contact.

Newcastle attacking with more urgency since conceding, but there are moans and groans in the ground at a misplaced Elanga pass. Sean Neave has just replaced Woltemade, and the 19-year-old wins a free-kick in a crossing position with his first action of the game.

The striker has only been on the pitch a few minutes, but Boniface has restored Leverkusen’s lead. Lovely chop inside the box, which sent Steur for a hot dog, before passing the ball into the far corner. No celebration of note from a player who could be on the move this summer.

Newcastle making just their second change of the game: Pivas replaces Mason Miley at right-back.

Leverkusen have made two more changes: Moreira and Maza off, Tella and Boniface on.

The corner is straight down the throat of Flekken, and that prompsts some groans from the home fans.

Newcastle having to defend deep for long periods, but Elanga did well to win a free-kick with little support. Moreira dragged the winger down. Then Wissa’s cross is turned behind for a corner.

Woltemade’s control lets him down as he tries to bring the ball down on halfway. The game is being played at a snail’s pace at the moment, but Leverkusen are dominating the ball.

Play has now resumed. Garcia does well to defend after Lewis Hall won the ball back in a dangerous position.

Time for another hydration break and Leverkusen are making three more substitutions. We await further changes from Jaissle. Should the game finish level, there will be a penalty shoot-out to decide the winner of the Visit Malta Cup.

Rather like the mid-week friendly against Everton, Newcastle have faded after half-time. Struggling to get into the game in any meaningful way. Slick football from Leverkusen but Fernandez fails to bring the ball under his spell in the box when there was time and space to shoot.

Leverkusen just inches away from regaining the lead. It was an incisive run off the left from Afonso Moreira, who tried to place the ball into the far corner but his attempt rolled just wide of the post.

Good defensive header by Lewis Hall before Wissa wins a foul on halfway. Newcastle feeding off scraps at the moment. Elanga goes too early and is flagged offside.

Bayer Leverkusen have had the better of it in this half, but some of the shooting has been wayward. This time is it Schik’s turn to slash a shot over the bar. Fouls committed by Finneran and Botman.

Newcastle with a three-on-three on the break after Wissa does well to win the ball back on halfway, but Woltemade was too slow to get his shot away at the end of the move. More good play from Wissa.

Half a chance for Fernandez to shoot from the edge of the D, but he was leaning back and ballooned the shot miles over the bar.

Finneran, the youngster in Newcastle’s midfield, is caught on the ball but then does well to recover it. I reckon there will be a raft of changes on the hour mark.

Corner for Leverkusen after Moreira gets forward and attacks Mason Miley. The German side have additional aerial threat with Schik on the pitch. Woltemade does well to head clear.

Bayer Leverkuen kick off in the second half.

Jaissle made 10 against Everton, so wants his starters to build minutes today. Rory Finneran is coming on for Newcastle, an 18-year-old academy player. He replaces Lewis Miley in midfield. Czech striker Patrik Schik is on for Bayer Leverkusen.

The scoreline is a fair reflection of an even first half, with Wissa Newcastle’s best player. The story though, is that kit clash that prompted Newcastle to change into their lilac third kit halfway through the half.

Just the two minutes of stoppage time to play.

Newcastle equalise from a set-piece. Flekken is claiming a foul, but it is a legitimate goal. The goalkeeper was nowhere to be seen on a corner that looped all the way to be back post, and he seemed to lose his bearings allowing Thiaw to find the far corner.

Newcastle have a corner after another move in which Wissa was lively. His performances have been a ray of light in pre-season, he really struggled in his first season at the club.

Lewis Hall takes the free-kick, but he scoops it well over the bar. Elanga delivers a low cross from the right, but Garcia is well positioned to clear.

Newcastle enjoying a lot more possession now, but you cannot say they look like equalising.

That was better though, more zip in the attack with Elanga laying the ball off for Wissa and Fernandez is booked from dragging the Newcastle forward to the ground. Free-kick in a shooting position.

Good play from Lewis Hall, skipping beyond two challenges to escape from a tight spot but then his crossfield pass is intercepted. Moreira passes the ball straight out of play for a Newcastle goal kick, when there was a chance for Leverkusen to punish the hosts on the break.

Elanga tries to take on Gutierrez but his low cross is too close to Flekken. Gutierrez then buys a foul when under pressure from Lewis Miley. Game has become quite bitty following those stoppages. Maza then chops down Harvery Barnes.

The game is back under way. Changing kits has improved things visually but it is still not ideal. You wonder how on earth two clubs of this stature failed to liaise on this before the game.

Bayer Leverkusen are still on top, but play has been stopped for a hydration break. Some boos from the stands, it is not an especially hot day.

On the subject of the kit clash, Newcastle are now changing into their lilac away kit. Shades of Manchester United at the Dell all those years ago.

A short stoppage in play after Tapsoba receives a knock in the small of the back from Newcastle’s goalkeeper Hornicek. Both managers get their players over for a tactical conflab.

Leverkusen look very accomplished in possession, they are moving the ball well through the lines. Kofane was a big threat when they played Arsenal in last season’s Champions League and they are looking to find him with crosses. Mason Miley defends well at right-back, but at the expense of a corner.

Flekken called into action again, Newcastle starting to warm to their task. It was direct play from first Elanga and then Barnes, but his cross deflects towards the goalkeeper and he parries away. Then Barnes is fouled, and Newcastle have a free-kick in a crossing position near the left corner of the penalty area. Poor delivery from Barnes, Flekken claims.

Newcastle fans sing “walking in a Keegan wonderland” in unison. Bade is then penalised for catching Woltemade late as they contested an aerial challenge.

Newcastle’s best moment so far: Wissa peels off the shoulder of Bade and tested Flekken with a volley from a tight angle. The goalkeeper saved and Leverkusen scramble clear, but it was good movement from the Newcastle striker.

Leverkusen continue to make the running, enjoying more possession and most of it is coming inside Newcastle’s half. Goalkeeper Flekken takes a beat inside his own six-yard box, and his pass out is almost cut out by Woltemade.

Newcastle’s players are wearing black armbands in memory of Kevin Keegan.

There is a slightly awkward clash of kits on display: both shirts feature a lot of white, and the blue trim around the shoulders of Newcastle’s home kit is quite similar to Leverkusen’s away strip.

Kofane, who impressed up front last season in Germany, throws himself at a cross.

Fans were barely settled in their seats when Maza’s vicious left-footed strike from outside of the area flew past Hornicek. Cracking goal, not much the goalkeeper could do about it.

Matthias Jaissle walks to the home dugout for the first time as manager. Just eight days until the proper stuff begins against Liverpool, a fixture which tends to throw up entertaining games. Bayer Leverkusen keep the home players waiting in the tunnel.

The former Liverpool defender has been linked with a move to Arsenal this week. Quansah is with his team-mates but not part of the matchday squad.

Bayer Leverkusen XI: Flekken; Gutierrez, Bade, Fernandez, Moreira, Tillman, Tapsoba, Arthur, Garcia, Maza, Kofane

Subs: Blaswich, Lomb, Hofmann, Terrier, Schick, Oermann, Tape, Poku, Vazquez, Boniface, Tella, Alfa-Ruprecht, Doganay, Hawighorst

Newcastle XI: Hornicek; M Miley, Thiaw (c), Botman, Hall; Steur, L Miley; Elanga, Woltemade, Barnes; Wissa

Subs: Harris, Charlton, Pivas, Sanusi, Johnson, Finneran, Neave

Today's team to take on Bayer Leverkusen in the @VisitMalta Weekender 👊 pic.twitter.com/ZfRvucBXSq

Newcastle United continue their preparations for the new season with a home friendly against Bayer Leverkusen, hoping to improve on their pretty limp showing against Everton at Murrayfield.

New manager ​Matthias Jaissle is ‌refusing to dwell on the departure of key players that has left his club in turmoil going into the Premier League season, insisting that he sees opportunity in the situation. Jaissle was recruited from Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli after Eddie Howe left last month, with the German coach joining a club who had lost Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and captain Bruno Guimaraes in quick succession.

“It’s a challenge, a big challenge, always when there’s a transitional period. ‌But it’s ‌not time to ⁠complain, it doesn’t make sense to see the negative things,” Jaissle said.

“We want to see the chance in that situation and that’s our approach from day one. We are here to do our ⁠best job. We want to support the players, the current squad.

“There will be adjustments to see in the coming days, weeks. But for now it’s only focused on the daily work, the work we can influence. That’s all that ​matters now.”

The 38-year-old coach arrived in Newcastle ‌having won two Austrian Bundesliga titles with Red Bull Salzburg before leading Al-Ahli to back-to-back AFC Champions League crowns.

He remained tight-lipped about new signings.

“Obviously, in that transition phase, the players who left the club were ‌great ​players, great characters, experienced ⁠players. This is now a vacuum,” he said.

“Either we adjust something in the squad, by signing these players, these profiles, or other players ⁠need to step up and fill ​these positions, these leadership roles. I’m quite optimistic, we can work in both scenarios.”

Jaissle said he had a ​clear vision of how he wants his team to play.

“The phrase how Newcastle ‌should play like is front-footed, intense, ​aggressive and of course also successful. ​In the end, it’s all about what ⁠I can ⁠say and it’s also why I’m sitting here,” he said.

“The approach we have as a coaching team and the identity of Newcastle is famed for, it’s so linked so close together - which is a perfect fit in my eyes and ​that’s going to be exciting.”

#2091. ‘If I stayed…’ – Rio Ngumoha reflects on ‘no-brainer’ decision to swap Chelsea for Liverpool

Rio Ngumoha has said that his decision to swap Chelsea for Liverpool in 2024 was a ‘no-brainer’.

The Reds signed the teenage winger from the London club’s academy just after he turned 16, with a subsequent tribunal determining that the Merseysiders were to pay an initial £2.8m (potentially rising to £6.8m) in compensation.

The now 18-year-old has gone on to make 44 appearances and counting for LFC’s first team, along with winning three senior England caps, and he’s turned in some man-of-the-match performances at Champions League level.

In a recent media interview (via The Standard), Ngumoha explained that he decided to leave Chelsea for Liverpool because he saw a clearer pathway to the first team at Anfield than he did in west London.

The winger said: “I needed a new challenge. I feel like if I stayed at Chelsea… not saying I wouldn’t have got to the first team as quickly, because I believe in my ability, but I feel Liverpool just gave me a new pathway.

“The plan they set for me was straightforward. For me, it was a no-brainer going to Liverpool.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

The Reds have had a fine track record for attracting top-class teenage talents in recent years, and Ngumoha is perhaps the standout signing in that category.

That Liverpool were prepared to go through a rigorous registration process with the Premier League (as the winger was a minor at the time) shows just how determined they were to see the deal through, and all of that bureaucratic effort has proven to be more than worth it.

In little more than a year, the teenager has gone from highly-rated prospect to established first-team presence, and there’s a palpable excitement among the fans at Anfield every time he gets the ball, with many a defender bamboozled by his phenomenal dribbling ability and supreme self-confidence.

Ngumoha’s leap of faith in joining the Reds has been vindicated by his regularity of senior football, especially this season as he’s started almost half of our matches across all competitions, and full credit to him for seizing his opportunity when it’s been handed to him.

Chelsea’s loss has very much proven to be our gain, and with the 18-year-old now holding a market value of €50m (£41.8m), that aforementioned compensation fee looks increasingly like one of the steals of the century.

£190 million raised from the sale of just four players certainly kept the accountants happy, whilst fans have had to deal with the anguish that comes from watching former favourites turn out for clubs who once were West Ham’s rivals.

One player in particular looks to be about to realise his stated ambition: Whilst he was still a Hammer, El Hadji Malick Diouf made no secret of his desire to play for a ‘top club’ one day – which didn’t exactly endear him to Irons supporters.

#2089. Jussi Jääskeläinen praises Arsenal star David Raya

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Former Premier League goalkeeper Jussi Jääskeläinen thinks David Raya is the best goalkeeper in the division right now.

But the former Bolton Wanderers star feels the Arsenal No.1 has more to prove before he can be put up with the all-time greats of the competition.

Jääskeläinen recently spoke to Kasinopartio.com, where he praised Raya’s performances and the understanding he has developed with Arsenal’s defenders.

“Raya has been a fantastic signing. He has a great relationship with the centre-backs; even when the back four changes, everything works well.”

The Spaniard has played a key role for Mikel Arteta since his arrival from Brentford. His organisation of the backline, key saves and contribution to Arsenal’s build up play have helped him to be a standout player.

In 2012, Raya began his journey in English football when he moved to Blackburn Rovers from Spain. At that time, he was just a young teenager unfamiliar with English football.

His short spell at Southport introduced him to senior football. Soon, he returned to Blackburn and forged a career ahead of moving to Brentford in 2019. After four years with Brentford, Raya achieved success at the club, helping them to the Premier League.

The player’s performances in the higher leagues caught the attention of Arsenal, and Arteta signed him on loan to the Emirates in 2023 before making the move permanent the following summer.

It didn’t take long for Raya to establish himself in the team. He took home the Premier League Golden Glove, having achieved 16 clean sheets in 32 appearances.

This was a significant milestone in his first season with the Arsenal team, and he has since remained as number one, playing a key role in the club’s pursuit of titles.

While Jääskeläinen said Raya is the best goalkeeper in the Premier League at the moment, he does not think he should be up there with the most experienced.

He believes other goalkeepers have earned an advantage through their consistency over a longer period.

“You have lots of top goalkeepers that I think are still a little bit ahead because of the years they’ve done it in the Premier League.”

“He’s not up there with them yet, but he’s definitely going in the right direction.”

Raya has already proven he can play to the top standard. However, it will be his consistency moving forward that will define his long-term reputation.

Petr Čech, Peter Schmeichel and Edwin van der Sar have all gained great reputations over the years. There is still plenty of time for Raya to do the same, but he will need to keep up his high standards whilst wearing an Arsenal shirt.

At just 31, Raya has a lot left in his career. If he can continue playing at this level, it will make the debate around whether he is one of the best goalkeepers in the Premier League even more intriguing.

#2088. West Ham Defender’s Remarkable Numbers Reveal January Transfer Problem

A recent X post by Luke, better known as LouOrns, showed some Championship centre-back analysis revealing that despite our shaky defence, Konstantinos Mavropanos is doing things that almost nobody else in the division can.

Looking at defenders with over 700 minutes played, the data shows a league dominated by specialists. Some centre-backs win everything in the air but struggle to contribute in possession. Others are comfortable progressing the ball but lack the physical dominance required to thrive in the Championship. Mavropanos is a rare exception. Winning more than 83% of his aerial duels while also posting progressive passing numbers comfortably above the league average, the Greek international combines two qualities that are rarely found in the same player. Only Portsmouth’s Regan Poole comes close to matching that balance, underlining just how unique Mavropanos’ profile has become.

What makes Mavropanos particularly impressive is that he is far more than a defender who simply attacks long balls. His progressive passing numbers are comfortably above the Championship average.

While defenders such as Billy Koumetio (Charlton), Ben Cabango (Swansea) and Nasser Djiga (Wolves) provide a respectable balance, none can match the Greek’s combination of aerial superiority and distribution.

That balance is precisely what makes him such a valuable asset. In a division built on physical battles, second balls and direct football, having a centre-back who consistently wins first contact whilst also driving possession forward provides a clear competitive edge, though it needs another three defenders and a goalkeeper to follow suit!

Dinos has posted some seriously impressive numbers

The chart paints a simple picture: many defenders excel at one aspect of the game. Very few excel at both.

And the data still doesn’t tell the full story.

What the chart does not show is goals. Mavropanos has already contributed five goals this season, an outstanding return for a central defender and further evidence of his all-round impact.

The Greek colossus is one of the rare exceptions to the rule, a centre-back performing at the very highest Championship standard.

West Ham are expected to receive January bids, and with a season drifting towards mid-table obscurity, may struggle to persuade our one and only key defender to remain at the London Stadium.

#2087. Mikel Merino speaks out on Arsenal role as January rumours grow

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Merino has played down any speculation around his potential exit during January. He has made it clear he will fight to keep his place in the squad.

He also spoke about speculation around Martin Zubimendi, who has been linked with Atletico Madrid.

Both players have been questioned over their role in Mikel Arteta’s midfield. There is increasing competition for positions at the Emirates.

Merino feels that there is always an intense fight for places in top-level football. He spoke about how strong and deep Arsenal are ahead of their Nations League clash against the Czech Republic.

Both Merino and Zubimendi were also keen to stress that they will be looking to gain more opportunities and not get distracted.

Merino has had to adapt to his new role at Arsenal after playing a key role on his team’s side. However, Merino has struggled to get into the starting XI.

He admitted that he wants to play more games. However, he acknowledged that it was difficult to get into the team, as there are so many quality players.

This shows that his playing time has not affected his relationship with Arteta.

Merino was able to understand what it is like to be a manager because his father was a football coach. He understands that tough decisions have to be made when selecting your starting XI.

This can be an important aspect in a difficult season, as all players need to play their part to make sure Arsenal stay challenging in multiple competitions.

Merino’s comments are very interesting considering the uncertainty around Zubimendi.

There are reports Zubimendi has been linked to Atletico Madrid and whether he will be looking to move in January.

Merino didn’t give a definite answer that these players will stay at Arsenal, but the comments do suggest they are looking to improve their position in the squad.

He also underlined the importance of having good cover, with Spain boss Luis de la Fuente believing players coming off the bench can be just as vital as those starting.

This is something Arsenal will want their squad to take on board. They will not always be able to play the same midfielders due to the demands of playing in both domestic and European competitions.

There is still time for Merino and Zubimendi to turn their situation around, so what they are doing now may not indicate how important they are going to be in the campaign.

Arsenal will be keen to keep Merino happy, and he has made his position clear. This should give some reassurance ahead of the January transfer window.

#2086. West Ham Insider Reveals Recruitment Mess Behind Club’s Decline

West Ham United are still suffering because of years of bad recruitment, Claret & Hugh has been told by a Hammers insider today. The source, who did not wish to be named, described the situation as a mess and laid the blame for the club’s current predicament firmly and squarely at muddled, poor recruitment.

Speaking to Claret & Hugh, the source said:

“It’s all down to recruitment and it’s been bad, a real mess.”

“It’s a hodge podge with players being brought from everywhere by loads of different people. We’re years behind and needed a complete reset, we had to start again and consider how we recruit.”

Honest words, and not ones that many West Ham fans would disagree with. The club has spent years changing managers, recruitment chiefs and transfer strategies, seemingly without allowing any one approach enough time to work. The result is a squad assembled under several different regimes, with little evidence of a consistent long-term plan.

It has always been Daniel Křetínský’s wish at West Ham to have a director of football in charge, and whilst we don’t have that exact job title at the club currently, Nils Koppen, as Director of Player Recruitment, is as good as a director of football in all but name.

What is clear is that the club are going to have to rebuild the recruitment structure brick by brick. And it’s worth pointing out that even as recently as the summer, there was still something of a mix-up, with a blend of recruitment ideas and Nuno Espírito Santo being allowed to bring in three players in Joël Piroe, Manor Solomon and Morato.

Kretinsky is a big believer in the structured recruitment model

That is hardly the definition of a joined-up recruitment strategy, although it’s also important to recognise that Koppen arrived with very little time to prepare for the summer window. The bigger issue is whether West Ham are finally prepared to commit to a consistent approach rather than changing direction whenever the manager changes.

We’re semi-lucky in one respect because we do have another transfer window coming up in January, giving Koppen and Scott Parker an opportunity to address some of the more obvious problems within the squad.

But this is definitely a time when West Ham have to commit to a transfer policy and allow it to play out and bear fruit over a number of seasons. Toying with an approach and then giving up, as we did with both Tim Steidten and Kyle Macaulay, is precisely the sort of short-term thinking that has contributed to the problem.

The club cannot keep appointing recruitment specialists, allowing them to start rebuilding the squad and then abandoning the entire project when results turn sour. At some point, West Ham have to decide what sort of players they want, how they’re going to identify them and who is ultimately responsible for bringing them in.

January offers an opportunity to begin correcting some of the mistakes, but the problems described by our source won’t be fixed in a single transfer window. If West Ham are genuinely years behind in their recruitment, the rebuild needs to be given the time and consistency that previous attempts have lacked.

Liverpool fans have been advised that prospective contract renewals for Virgil van Dijk and Alisson Becker could take time to materialise.

The future of both long-serving players has been in the spotlight this week after they publicly addressed their respective situations, with the goalkeeper’s agent already in talks with club chiefs while the captain has maintained a more neutral ‘let’s see’ stance.

Their current deals are set to expire next June, and they’ll be able to sign pre-contract agreements with overseas clubs from the beginning of January unless they extend their terms with the Reds before then.

The journalist explained how Liverpool would need to take a pragmatic approach to the renewal process and not be led by sentiment, with the defender turning 36 next July and the goalkeeper’s 35th birthday coming three months later.

In a more hopeful note, Pearce wrote: ‘It makes sense for all parties to wait and see how things unfold in the coming weeks and months. Respect abounds and relationships are strong, with dialogue ongoing between sporting director Julian Ward and the pair’s camps.’

Beltrán has enjoyed an impressive breakthrough season, making 45 appearances and keeping 19 clean sheets, while also earning recognition from the Argentina national team.

The reported interest comes at an interesting time for West Ham, with Scott Parker facing an increasingly obvious problem between the posts. However, I would suggest the goalkeeper situation is only one of two major priorities for Nils Koppen when the January transfer window opens.

West Ham sold more than £200 million worth of players during the summer transfer window and spent just under £40 million on recruitment. Therefore, I would already hope that there is money set aside for January, rather than it becoming a straight choice between signing a goalkeeper or a striker.

Koppen wants to sign a goalkeeper in January

The problems in front of goal have been well documented, with Koppen already making enquiries about potential replacements for Taty Castellanos. But the goalkeeping situation is arguably just as concerning, as the numbers surrounding Mads Hermansen make increasingly uncomfortable reading.

As for the reported US$15 million valuation of Beltrán, I’m not going to sit here and pretend I’ve watched the goalkeeper play. I haven’t, and I’m certainly not going to offer a technical assessment of somebody I haven’t properly studied.

#2082. Scott Parker’s West Ham Training Plans Hit By International Call-Ups

Much has been made of the two-week international break giving Scott Parker his first proper opportunity to work with his West Ham players. Having taken charge just before the Cardiff City match, the new Hammers manager has barely had time to get his feet under the table, let alone implement his preferred tactics.

However, the truth is that Parker’s supposed two-week opportunity on the training pitch is nowhere near as useful as it sounds. West Ham have had ten first-team squad members called up for international duty, leaving the manager without several players who would ordinarily be involved in his starting XI.

Mads Hermansen, Tomáš Souček, Konstantinos Mavropanos, Manor Solomon, Joël Piroe and Mohamadou Kanté have all been selected for senior international duty. Edvin Austbø, Divine Mukasa, Airidas Golambeckis and Finlay Herrick were also named in age-group squads, although Herrick has subsequently withdrawn from England’s Under-20 squad, with the FA citing ‘injury’ as the reason.

That leaves Parker with a rather makeshift group of players to work with, although it should at least provide opportunities for others to press their claims for a starting place.

Assuming everybody is fit and available, the following is a possible starting eleven Parker could assemble on the training ground during the international break.

It’s not a bad group of players by any means, and the likes of Lewis Orford and Josh Ajala should welcome the chance to impress their new manager. However, it’s a long way from the team Parker is likely to select when West Ham face Preston North End.

Even something as straightforward as drilling the defence is going to be difficult. Whilst Morato can slot into a makeshift back four alongside Kilman, the likelihood is that Mavropanos will be Parker’s preferred centre-back when everybody is available.

And even if Mavropanos were to suffer an injury, I’d expect Golambeckis to be considered ahead of Morato. Unfortunately, both players are away representing their countries, meaning Parker cannot even work with what I suspect will be his first-choice defensive partnership or its most likely alternative.

It’s a similar story further forward, where Mukasa, Kanté, Austbø and Piroe are all missing. These are players Parker will need to assess and integrate into his preferred system, yet he’ll have precious little opportunity to do so before the Preston match.

Of course, there are positives. Parker can still work on his overall shape, passing patterns and defensive organisation, whilst giving some of the younger players an opportunity to impress.

But the idea that West Ham’s new manager has been handed two uninterrupted weeks to transform his team is somewhat misleading. He has time on the training pitch, certainly, but not with many of the players he’ll actually need when the Championship resumes.

West Ham midfielder Tomáš Souček has admitted that the players must take their share of responsibility for the club’s disappointing Championship campaign, insisting that changing the manager doesn’t absolve them of blame.

#2080. Independent Football Regulator approve West Ham board appointment

The Independent Football Regulator has approved James Taylor as West Ham’s new CFO, who can now join the West Ham board as company secretary and a director.

He replaces Andy Mollet, who retired in the summer after 14 years at West Ham.

IFR Outcome: The IFR determined that James Taylor is suitable for the role of Officer at West Ham United.

James Taylor (the applicant) submitted an application to the IFR for approval to carry out the role of SMF3: Chief Finance Function at West Ham United Football Club Limited (West Ham United).

Having assessed the application, under section 29 of the Football Governance Act 2026 (the Act), the IFR has determined that the applicant is suitable to be an officer, SMF3: Chief Finance Function, of West Ham United.

This means that, having considered the factors in section 37 of the Act and the IFR’s ODSE Rules, the IFR has concluded that the applicant:

Under section 82 of the Act, a person whom the IFR considers is directly affected by an IFR suitability determination may ask for it to be reviewed by a committee of the IFR Board who were not involved in making the original determination.

Any request must be made within 7 days of this determination’s publication date (or, if earlier, the date on which the IFR notified that person of this determination).

Further guidance on who the IFR may consider to be directly affected by its determinations, and how to request a review, can be found here.

After any requested review has been conducted, a concerned person, or other person with a sufficient interest, has a further right under section 84 of the Act to appeal the reviewer’s decision to the Competition Appeal Tribunal.

The IFR was formed in 2025 and includes former West Ham Executive Director Tara Warren as a non-executive director on its board.

#2079. Ambition, decency and temptation to watch Manchester United pantomime with certain satisfaction

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

There is a temptation, as a Newcastle United fan, to watch the pantomime at Manchester United with a certain satisfaction.

Those of us who remember Manchester United looking down on everyone else can hardly be expected to overlook the irony.

But watching the uncertainty surrounding Michael Carrick at Old Trafford, my overriding reaction is that I would hate to see our own club conducting its business like this at St James’ Park.

Carrick has continued reporting for work while his future has been debated in public and senior executives prepare to decide his fate elsewhere.

Reports of possible replacements have filled the space in between. Whatever the eventual decision, that is a miserable position in which to leave someone expected to lead a dressing room.

A fine footballer and, from everything I have seen of him, a thoroughly decent man deserves better. So does anyone asked to carry responsibility on behalf of a football club.

That does not mean Carrick should be immune from criticism. Being a distinguished former player does not guarantee that someone will become a successful manager. Being decent does not win matches. Results matter, and there comes a point when those running a club have to decide whether the person they appointed can deliver what is required.

But the manner in which they reach and communicate that decision tells us something about their own capability.

It is easy to look decisive when somebody else is being dismissed. The harder questions concern the judgement that put him there, the support he received and the part played by those now sitting in judgement.

Who chose the manager? What did they believe he could achieve? Were the players recruited suited to the football he was expected to produce? Were the expectations realistic? And if the appointment has failed, what have the people who made it learned?

Those questions should survive the departure of any manager. Too often, the departure itself seems to make them disappear.

The manager leaves, a new man arrives, and everyone above him gets to talk about a fresh start.

I have spent my working life in businesses, and one thing becomes clear over time: changing the person in charge of the operation will achieve very little if the people directing it cannot recognise their own contribution to its problems.

Football has a particular talent for obscuring that responsibility. The manager stands in front of the cameras. He explains the defeat, defends the players and answers questions about decisions he may have had only a limited part in making.

Those who set the budgets, shape the structure and approve the appointments are much less exposed.

That imbalance makes it all the more important that they behave properly.

If a manager retains your confidence, give him the backing necessary to do his job. If he has lost it, deal with the matter directly and respectfully. There will always be speculation in football. A well-run club should understand the damage caused when speculation becomes the dominant account of its leadership.

How much authority can a manager exercise when everyone around him is wondering whether he will still be there next week?

That is the lesson I want Newcastle United to take from all this.

We are entitled to ambition. We are entitled to question performances, recruitment and decisions. Supporting Newcastle does not oblige any of us to suspend our judgement, and a club with serious aspirations cannot avoid difficult choices.

But I want those choices made by people who understand what they are responsible for, who can explain the direction of the club and who have enough conviction to hold their course through a difficult spell.

Patience needs a purpose. It should rest on evidence that the work is sound, that the people involved can improve things and that the club is moving towards something coherent. Equally, a change of manager needs more justification than the desire to relieve the pressure for a few weeks.

Before making that change, the people running Newcastle should be able to explain what has failed, why a replacement would have a better chance and what they themselves will do differently.

Otherwise, we are simply buying another turn on the same roundabout.

As someone who has supported Newcastle United all his life, I know how readily hope can attach itself to the next appointment. We have all imagined the press conference, the first signing, the first stirring performance. We have all wanted to believe that this time the right man has arrived.

But a manager needs a club capable of helping him succeed. He needs sound recruitment, clear responsibilities and people around him whose judgement adds something when results become difficult. Above all, he needs to know that support inside the building is real.

Supporters need something similar. We do not need to know every private conversation. We do need confidence that somebody is thinking beyond the next headline.

Respect matters here, too. People can fall short in a job and still deserve to leave with their dignity intact. A club reveals its standards in how it treats someone whose usefulness to it may be coming to an end. That should matter to supporters who care about the institution as well as the team.

Watching Michael Carrick caught in this public uncertainty, I find myself thinking less about Manchester United’s next manager than about the people responsible for creating the circumstances in which he must work. Their decisions deserve scrutiny every bit as much as his team selections.

Let others enjoy the Old Trafford spectacle if they wish. For Newcastle United, there is something more useful to take from it.

We should expect ambition from those entrusted with our great club. We should also expect judgement, accountability and the basic decency to treat people properly.

The next time Newcastle United face a difficult run, those expectations will matter far more than anything said when the going was good.

#2078. Scott Parker Must Restore West Ham’s Most Dangerous Weapon

One of the most disappointing aspects of West Ham’s performance against Blackburn Rovers at the weekend was the fact that Jarrod Bowen didn’t drift into the middle and cause havoc in the way he had against Cardiff City. Having watched what happened in Wales, I was genuinely excited about the possibilities for our captain under Scott Parker.

Because make no mistake about it, one of the biggest reasons the Hammers were able to overturn a three-goal deficit against Cardiff was the freedom afforded to Bowen. No longer was he restricted to the right wing, and suddenly he was popping up in central areas of the pitch, having a hand in all three West Ham goals.

As a result, I thought we might have discovered something rather special. Bowen could start on the right wing but effectively be given licence to operate as a number ten, providing West Ham with a completely different attacking threat. It was a whole new Jarrod Bowen, and he was incredibly effective at it.

That’s why I was so disappointed to see Bowen playing as a conventional, orthodox right winger against Blackburn. Having witnessed how dangerous he could be when drifting into central areas, I really thought Parker would look to exploit that again.

Instead, Bowen spent much of the match operating in his familiar position, and West Ham lost the unpredictability which had made him so effective against Cardiff. Of course, Blackburn were different opponents, but I couldn’t help feeling we’d missed a trick.

West Ham captain Bowen looked brilliant when seemingly given a free role against Cardiff City

The interesting thing is that I don’t believe Bowen needs to become an out-and-out striker to solve this problem. In fact, moving him permanently into the number nine position could simply deprive West Ham of their best creative player.

What excited me against Cardiff wasn’t the prospect of Bowen replacing the centre-forward. It was the possibility of him playing both roles at different moments, starting wide before moving inside and creating problems that opposition defenders struggled to deal with.

For all West Ham’s attacking problems, we already have a player capable of making things happen. Bowen demonstrated that against Cardiff, and I would argue that his movement and creativity were every bit as important as the goals themselves.

There’s no reason why he cannot continue to provide width when required while also moving into the space behind the striker. That flexibility could be particularly valuable with Joël Piroe leading the line, giving West Ham somebody to finish the opportunities Bowen creates.

I don’t want to see Parker abandon something which worked so spectacularly after just 45 minutes. We’ve spent much of this season struggling to create chances, yet against Cardiff we appeared to stumble upon a way of getting considerably more from our best player.

The international break gives Parker time to work on these attacking combinations, and I hope restoring Bowen’s freedom is near the top of his priorities. By the time West Ham face Preston North End, I’d like to see our captain operating with the same licence that made him almost unplayable in Cardiff.

#2077. “I don’t know why…” – John Aldridge fears Liverpool’s stance on one player could ‘backfire’

John Aldridge has questioned why Liverpool weren’t more assertive in pulling Dominik Szoboszlai out of national team duty when he’s currently nursing a minor injury.

The midfielder sprained his ankle in the 3-1 victory at Crystal Palace on Sunday, with Andoni Iraola uncertain after the game as to whether or not the 26-year-old would join up with his country during this international window.

In a statement on Tuesday, the Hungarian FA said that a decision on the player’s participation against Georgia and Northern Ireland over the next week will be deferred until the ‘last minute’ as his fitness continues to be assessed.

In his latest column for the Liverpool Echo, Aldridge voiced his belief that Liverpool should’ve done more to prevent Szoboszlai from playing for Hungary in the coming days when he’s clearly not fully fit.

The former Reds striker wrote: ‘I know Virgil van Dijk has pulled out of the Netherlands squad because of a little niggle, but Dominik Szoboszlai has stayed with Hungary despite injuring his knee against Palace.

‘Any other club would pull them out of international duty. Manchester United, Arsenal, Man City – they’d all pull them. We’ve seen it before. Any doubt and that’s it, decision made, you’re not playing. I don’t understand why we don’t throw our weight around like that.

‘I understand players want to play for their country. I was the same with Ireland. I would answer call-ups even when I was injured. I get what it means and how much it means to players, but any other club would just pull them. That’s not happened here, I don’t know why. Hopefully that just means it’s not that serious.

‘It still sounds like they’re taking a risk. If he stays with Hungary and plays, we’ve just got to hope the decision doesn’t backfire and come back to hurt Liverpool.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

As Szoboszlai is contracted to Liverpool, the Merseyside club could’ve blocked him from representing his country during this international window because of his knee injury.

However, it’d appear to be a case of the player wanting to at least link up with the Hungary camp and try to prove his fitness, and Anfield chiefs green-lighting that action out of respect for the 26-year-old and not wanting to antagonise him by forbidding him to travel.

The grey area over the midfielder potentially being fit enough to play but not certain of doing so has presented a tricky dilemma, as much as Iraola would no doubt have preferred for our number 8 to swerve national team duty and prioritise his club instead.

With Hungary not playing until Saturday, that does give Szoboszlai a bit of time to recover from the knee issue he incurred at Selhurst Park, and we’d like to think that Marco Rossi wouldn’t risk fielding him against Georgia unless he’s definitely OK to feature.

While a swift return to action for the 26-year-old would obviously be a good thing, we just hope it doesn’t come at the expense of his involvement for Liverpool in the coming weeks, especially with a hectic run of 11 matches in 40 days before the end of December.

Welcome to our Live Comments section, where new comments will appear automatically

It is all very well and good for pundits (code word for writers with preposterous assertions) to voice the opinion that LFC should have been more assertive in voicing their opinion on Szoboszlai not starting for Hungary. The problem with that line of thinking is that Szobo is always passionate to play for his country (and as seen last year in his performances to play for LFC), so if you deny him the right to play, you run the risk of alienating him, something Aldridge does not have to concern himself with because he has nothing to do with LFC or Szobo. I also worry that if he is allowed to start when not fit he will further injure himself, but believe Szobo and his manager will not take that action if he is not fit and can understand that Szobo as his country’s captain, if he does not start he would at least like to be on the sidelines giving his teammates moral support – something Aldridge also does not have to concern himself with!
