#2076. For Newcastle United fans who haven’t yet done so, I urge you to, because it’s excellent

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

“Hello, people of podland and beyond”, those were the words of fellow Mag writer Jamie Smith, as he introduced the inaugural episode of ‘The Mag Podcast’, back in August.

For those Newcastle United fans who haven’t yet listened, I urge you to do so, because it’s excellent.

We’re up to Episode 15 now and to date, Jamie has been joined for each episode by Simon Cahill, a southern convert to all things Newcastle United according to his Mag bio (he certainly sounds like he’s from down south) as well as the miserable mag himself, David Hutchinson, AKA Hutch (who sounds very much like a local).

Whilst Jamie and I have writing for The Mag in common, we don’t know each other and have only met each other in person once, but nonetheless, I have been heaping praise on him for most of the time after listening to each episode, including episodes 2 and 3, which I listened to high above the Atlantic Ocean as I flew in and out of New York on a family holiday (I reckoned that must have been a first for the pod).

I listen on Spotify, there are alternatives to this – Apple Podcasts, Amazon Music, YouTube if you like, and you can also play direct from the article that Simon routinely posts as each episode is released. I haven’t read a lot of comments from other Newcastle United fans about it, so it’s hard to get a handle on how The Mag Pod is being received. As I said earlier though, I think it’s marvellous.

During the past three months, the guys have navigated hugely important issues such as Manchester City’s alleged indiscretions with the 115 charges, and football’s loss of community with the increasing amount of commercial interests impinging on the beautiful game, as well as the possibility of new legislation to allow the consumption of alcohol in the stands.

Jamie, who speaks with a heavy Geordie accent but does so as eloquently as he writes, talked with passion to mark the passing of King Kev, The Mag podcast doing its very own tribute to the Messiah in episode 2.

I normally listen on my commute into work on the 21 bus. I often find myself laughing out loud, something that seems to make my fellow passengers extremely nervous from the looks I get when this invariably happens.

When discussing the 115 charges and potential punishments in episode 8, Jamie used the US justice system to illustrate how a massive points deduction for Man City would be as futile as those 500-year prison sentences they hand down in places like Alabama. That had me in stitches!

That was after Hutch had made a complete hash of introducing the Carabao Cup draw in episode 7, although in suggesting that we would lose to Fleetwood if we were to get them, he showed great foresight given that was Arsenal ‘s fate when they played at the other Highbury. Meanwhile, Simon was all over the place, when asked to read out the results from the Nations League matches during the international break.

In episode 9 (and you could tell that the International Break was grinding by this time) the guys even imagined themselves as Sam Beckett from the TV show Quantum Leap, in which they afforded themselves the opportunity to travel back in time in an attempt to change the course of history for Newcastle United.

The point here is that this isn’t easy, but they do a great job with humility and humour.

In the most recent episode (number 15) which has just aired, the lads gave their ratings on the season so far, Jamie and Simon going for D minus, with Hutch offering a marginally better assessment at D. I have to say, this did enrage me, particularly after my most recent article, ‘Lies, damn lies, and statistics (and Newcastle United)’ in which I made the case for Matthias Jaissle because we aren’t any worse off than last season and have in fact amassed a staggering five points more from our opponents these ten games into the season than was the case last time out in the corresponding fixtures. My own assessment, had I been asked – C plus (could do better but certainly not in special measures).

Had I also been asked to grade The Mag podcast, I’d be inclined to settle at a B; it’s still early days, but it’s improving week by week, the material is interesting, there is often humour and when I compare it to other Newcastle United podcasts I have listened to, I think it’s a whole lot better.

Call me biased if you want, but if you haven’t done so, give it a go and a big shout out to Jamie, Simon and Hutch, I’m already looking forward to episode 16. 🎙️ THE MAG PODCAST Ep 15: Fulham frustration, Newcastle United’s season report card and Relegation fears Listen to the latest episode of The Mag Pod! #2075. West Ham’s £20m Striker Has Two Weeks To Change Parker’s Mind

It would be fair to say that West Ham’s £20 million striker Pablo has been something of a victim of the club’s decision to sack Nuno Espírito Santo. As every Hammers fan knows, Nuno was a big fan of the Brazilian, who towards the end of his reign had moved to the top of the pecking order ahead of both Taty Castellanos and Joël Piroe.

Unfortunately for the former Gil Vicente forward, as soon as Scott Parker arrived, he dropped out of the squad altogether and didn’t appear to be anywhere near the first team. Pablo was absent from the matchday squads against both Cardiff City and Blackburn Rovers, despite having been a regular selection under the previous manager.

There are two possible reasons for this, in my opinion. The first, and probably most obvious, is that Parker simply doesn’t deem him good enough to warrant a first-team squad place ahead of Piroe or Castellanos. The second could be the Championship’s squad eligibility requirements, with Soungoutou Magassa returning to the picture and potentially leaving Pablo as the overseas-trained player to miss out.

Now, I’m not going to sit here and pretend to be Pablo’s biggest fan. That would be disingenuous of me, because I’ve been critical of his finishing, overall technique and I still don’t believe he scores enough goals.

But let’s be fair, neither does Taty Castellanos, yet it always seems to be poor old Pablo who takes the brunt of the blame. Whatever his shortcomings in front of goal, nobody could reasonably question his work rate, which was clearly one of the reasons Nuno valued his pressing and willingness to chase lost causes.

The Brazilian could now be one of the unexpected beneficiaries of West Ham having so many players away on international duty. As things stand, Parker doesn’t have enough senior players available to put out a balanced eleven, even in a training match, which could provide Pablo with an opportunity to impress.

With Piroe representing Suriname and both of West Ham’s left-wing options, Manor Solomon and Edvin Austbø, also away with their countries, Parker has considerably fewer attacking players to work with than he would ordinarily expect.

Taty and Pablo will need to perform in training

It could therefore be that Pablo has a couple of weeks to impress his new boss, which in terms of effort and application I’ve little doubt he’ll do. The real question is whether Parker believes the striker possesses the necessary technique to operate within his preferred system.

After all, hard work should be a prerequisite rather than a reason for anybody to get into the team. And given Parker’s drive and intensity, I suspect everybody will be working hard once he has the opportunity to properly implement his methods.

But with West Ham’s pressing, or lack of it, also under the microscope, it could well be that Parker eventually chooses to select Pablo for exactly the same reasons Nuno Espírito Santo always did.

Pablo might not be the most technically gifted striker at the club, and his goalscoring record certainly leaves plenty to be desired. Nevertheless, if Parker wants somebody prepared to harass defenders, chase down possession and lead the press from the front, he already has a player who has demonstrated a willingness to do precisely that.

Whether that’s enough to earn him another chance remains to be seen, but the international break could provide an unexpected opportunity for a striker who appeared to have been completely forgotten.

#2073. West Ham’s £22m Question As Koppen’s Signings Come Under Scrutiny

Following information received by Claret & Hugh from a football agent that West Ham’s biggest problem has been recruitment, I thought it would be worth taking a closer look at the summer business conducted under Director of Player Recruitment Nils Koppen.

The argument that West Ham’s entire recruitment process needs rebuilding from the ground up is certainly an interesting one, and appointing somebody to oversee that operation is an obvious starting point. Koppen is effectively operating as a director of football, even if his official job title is slightly different, and his work will be crucial to the club’s future.

For the purposes of this assessment, I’ve concentrated on five players I understand to have been Koppen’s choices. I’ve left out Manor Solomon, Joël Piroe and Morato, whom I understand were specifically wanted by Nuno Espírito Santo, along with Keiber Lamadrid, who was already at the club last season and whose recruitment I understand was driven by David Sullivan.

It’s worth remembering that Koppen was hardly afforded the luxury of a full summer to plan his first transfer window. He arrived at West Ham on 4 July and explained in an interview with the club’s official Iron Cast podcast that his usual recruitment planning had to be dramatically accelerated.

Koppen described putting together an 80-day plan focused on executing the summer window, when ideally he would have preferred a much longer period to assess players and prepare. That’s important context when judging the business, particularly given the number of players West Ham needed to bring in.

Nevertheless, the signings are now here, and we’ve had an opportunity to watch them. It’s probably too early to place too much emphasis on any individual player, but we can at least begin to assess what Koppen has delivered and what supporters might expect from his recruitment in January.

I’ll start with Joël Veltman, who I think has been a really solid signing. He brings bags of experience, understands the defensive side of the game and would currently be my choice as West Ham’s best right-back.

Given that he arrived on a free transfer, I struggle to see how anybody could argue against this deal. Veltman was particularly impressive during the second half against Cardiff City, and his composure could become increasingly important under Scott Parker.

For me, this was an absolute no-brainer and one of the clearest positives from Koppen’s summer business.

Veltman has been a decent signing for West Ham

Unfortunately, I think quite the opposite can be said about Adama Boiro. He was clearly some way down West Ham’s list of preferred targets, and his failure to establish himself suggests this particular recruitment decision hasn’t worked.

I’m prepared to give the club a little leeway because I genuinely believe they expected El Hadji Malick Diouf to remain at West Ham for this campaign. That would have changed the urgency surrounding the left-back position and perhaps explains why the eventual recruitment looked rather improvised.

What is clear is that Nuno Espírito Santo didn’t appear to consider Boiro good enough for regular first-team football. I’d also be very surprised if he manages to break into Scott Parker’s starting XI, and therefore it’s difficult to regard his arrival as a good signing.

Divine Mukasa is a completely different proposition, and I think bringing him in on loan from Manchester City was an astute move. He’s clearly an exceptionally talented young footballer, and I believe there’s considerably more to come from him.

We’ve already seen glimpses of his ability, particularly during the comeback against Cardiff, when he scored and helped transform West Ham’s attacking play. He has the imagination and technical ability to make things happen, which is something this team has lacked far too often.

I actually think Mukasa could be one of the biggest beneficiaries of Parker having time to implement his ideas. Of course, the obvious downside is that he’s only on loan, but that doesn’t diminish the quality of the original recruitment decision.

Edvin Austbø is another player I think has enormous potential. The overall package was just under €15 million, but he’s on relatively modest wages, which is an important consideration when assessing the total cost of a transfer.

I’ve been encouraged by his directness, willingness to take on defenders and ability to make things happen. He looked particularly lively against Blackburn, and I was surprised when Parker decided to replace him with Manor Solomon.

There’s still plenty of development required, but that’s hardly surprising given his age. Austbø looks like a genuinely promising player, and if he continues improving, this could turn out to be an excellent piece of business.

His arrival also reflects the sort of recruitment markets Koppen knows well, with West Ham looking beyond the more obvious and expensive options for emerging talent.

Last but certainly not least is Arne Engels, the player from whom most is expected, and rightly so. At a reported £22 million, he became the most expensive signing in Championship history, so it’s perfectly reasonable to expect something special.

Nuno clearly liked him, and I suspect Parker will appreciate his qualities too. However, I’m still undecided about exactly what sort of player Engels is and what he does particularly well.

I would expect the most expensive player ever purchased in the Championship to excel at something, and I’m not entirely convinced Engels does. He’s a bit of an all-rounder, with bags of energy, decent passing ability and a willingness to get stuck in, but I’m still waiting to see that outstanding quality which justifies the fee.

That’s not to say he’s a bad player, because he certainly isn’t. He scored an excellent goal against Cardiff and has shown enough to suggest he could develop into a very useful midfielder, but I don’t yet know whether he’s the exceptional player West Ham paid exceptional money to acquire.

Indeed, if I could keep either Engels or Mukasa at the club next season, at this moment I’d actually choose Mukasa. That might change over the coming months, but it’s an indication of where I currently stand on the two players.

Overall, I think it’s fair to say Koppen’s first batch of signings has been a mixed bag. Veltman looks excellent value, Mukasa and Austbø have considerable potential, Boiro has been disappointing and Engels remains something of an unknown quantity.

However, I don’t believe we can reasonably judge somebody who is, for all intents and purposes, operating as a director of football after just one transfer window. Particularly not when he arrived with so little preparation time and was working alongside a manager who has since been dismissed.

I wouldn’t call Koppen’s recruitment a success or a failure at this stage. The jury is very much still out, and there’s every possibility that Austbø, Engels and Mukasa could enjoy excellent November and December performances under Parker.

If that happens, Koppen’s summer business could look considerably better by January without West Ham signing another player. Equally, if those players fail to develop, the questions surrounding his recruitment will become more difficult to ignore.

For now, it’s a case of watch this space. Koppen has made some encouraging decisions and some questionable ones, but his work deserves to be judged over a much longer period than a single summer transfer window.

Michael Carrick has now been sacked by Manchester United.

An official announcement on Thursday morning revealing the news.

The Geordie manager now the latest victim of Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers.

#2071. Rashford returns and Fernandes misses another penalty as Man Utd humbled by Amorim

Bruno Fernandes missed a penalty for the second successive pre-season friendly as Manchester United were beaten 4-2 by former head coach Ruben Amorim’s AC Milan.

Fernandes, who rolled a spot-kick wide in a shoot-out against Leeds in midweek, was gifted the chance to open his pre-season account in Wroclaw, Poland.

His effort was on target this time, but Milan keeper Lorenzo Torriani dived to his right to beat the shot away.

Fernandes did at least get an assist, taking the second-minute corner which was powerfully headed home by Harry Maguire to give United the lead.

Amorim’s Milan equalised after a defensive mix-up allowed Gonçalo Ramos to break into the area and square for Samuel Chukwueze to roll home.

United were awarded their penalty just before half-time after Koni De Winter tugged back Youri Tielemans, but Torriani guessed correctly to leave Fernandes frustrated.

United retook the lead after Patrick Dorgu pounced on a loose backpass from Filippo Terracciano, but Milan equalised again when Chukwueze’s wayward shot was poked in by Alphadjo Cissè at the far post.

Marcus Rashford, who was frozen out by Amorim and loaned out to Aston Villa and then Barcelona, came on as a substitute on the hour for his first United appearance since returning from Spain.

But Milan went ahead in the 68th minute when Chukwueze’s cross was headed home by Ramos, and three minutes later former Chelsea midfielder Ruben Loftus-Cheek raced through to hit the fourth and cap a performance that underlines United’s need for reinforcements before their season starts in earnest next Saturday, away at Hull City.

Manchester United (4-2-3-1) Lammens; Mazraoui (Dalot 61), Maguire, Heaven (Martinez 61), Shaw; Tielemans, Santos (Mainoo 61); Diallo (Lacey 61), Fernandes, Dorgu (Rashford 61); Cunha (Mbeumo 61). Subs Zirkzee, Yoro, J Fletcher, T Fletcher, Amass, Collyer, Mee (g), Heath (g), Gabriel. Booked Dorgu.

AC Milan (3-4-2-1) Torriani; Terracciano (Gila 60), Winter (Vladimirov 84), Pavlovic (Diawara 84); Chukwueze, Musah (Ricci 76), Jashari (Modric 60), Estupinan (Bartesaghi 61); Loftus-Cheek (Comotto 84), Cisse (Saelemaekers 60); Ramos (Camarda 75). Subs Pittarella (g), Bouyer (g). Booked Estupinan.

Goals Chukwueze (37), Cisse (57), Ramos (68), Loftus-Cheek (71).

That six-time Champions League winner Luka Modric raised the trophy with the one hand said everything you need to know about this moment...

Aug 30: Manchester United vs Ipswich Town

Sep 13: Manchester United vs Manchester City

United’s pre-season ends in defeat. A wretched second half proves their undoing as Amorim’s Milan score four. Worth reminding that United led this match, twice.

Milan are playing keep-ball in these latter stages and although Mainoo regains possession, his attempt to play forward is cut out and Modric’s outside-of-the-foot pass finds Comotto, who heads straight at Lammens.

Four minutes of added time to be played...

United now raining crosses down on Milan’s box but Torriani equal to it every time.

For the second time this afternoon, Shaw directs a lovely ball into Fernandes’ path in behind Milan’s back line, but the Portugal international can’t bring it under his spell.

Martinez has added a little bit of urgency to United’s build-up. Mbeumo tries to feed Shaw down the line but the ball is cut out.

More substitutions... Diawara, Vladimirov and Comotto enter the field of play in place of Pavlovic, De Winter and Loftus-Cheek.

Big chance for Rashford! Martinez lofts a fantastic ball over the top but Rashford is not quite able to bring it under his spell, with Torriani and De Winter combing to clear their lines.

Milan are now sitting off, settling into a back five as they look to preserve their advantage. Fernandes, Tielemans and Dalot combine well but such has been United’s fortunes this afternoon, the ball ricochets off the referee and play is halted.

Good work from Rashford in the corner to regain possession, but his ball into the box is not picked up by a team-mate.

More changes... Ramos and Musah make way for Camarda and Ricci.

Manchester United 2 AC Milan 4 (Loftus-Cheek) No sooner had the players returned after the second-half hydration break then Milan exploit United’s exposed left side (again). Ramos sends Loftus-Cheek through and the midfielder composes himself before bending the ball around Lammens.

Manchester United 2 AC Milan 3 (Ramos) That’s too easy. United fail to learn their lesson, Shaw not getting tight enough to Chukwueze and the winger’s cross is met by new signing Ramos, who powers a header back across goal and past Lammens.

Loftus-Cheek and Ramos are doing a good job of cutting off the pass into United’s midfield in their build-up phase.

Rashford (who makes his first United appearance in almost two years), Lacey, Dalot, Mbeumo, Mainoo and Martinez replace Dorgu, Amad, Mazraoui, Cunha, Santos and Heaven.

For Milan, Saelemaekers, Bartesaghi, Gila and Modric are on for Cisse, Estupinan, Terracciano and Jashari

Manchester United 2 AC Milan 2 (Cisse) United have set a higher defensive line so far this half, with their front line pressing with more intensity to avoid the ball over the top. However Chukwueze is able to find space around the sides, coming in off the right and curling an effort goalwards which Cisse turns in at the far post. There are calls for offside, but with no VAR here, the goal stands.

Milan win a free-kick some 25 yards out after Fernandes clips Estupinan. Teenager Cisse steps up and fires straight into the United wall. Was always going to be difficult to trouble Lammens from there.

Manchester United 2 AC Milan 1 (Dorgu) United wisely decide to keep hold of the ball for a while, the midfield three rotating to disrupt Milan’s out-of-possession shape and open up passing lanes. A Milan throw-in from the right-back berth is precedes an awful backpass by Terracciano which is pounced on by Dorgu who curls the ball beyond Torriani.

United have looked bright in the opening moments of this half. They win a free-kick midway into Milan’s half. The ball is delivered to the back post and, after some 18-yard-box pinball, a relieved Torriano pounces on it.

Both teams remain unchanged as the second 45 minutes begin.

All square at the break. Tough to know what to make of that half – United looked solid enough and could have taken a lead into the interval had Fernandes converted his penalty, but they failed to create a wealth of clear-cut chances. It will be interesting to see how Carrick approaches this second half.

Milan have enjoyed just a tick over two-thirds of possession, which United have contributed to in part through some lackadaisical passing.

Fernandes misses a spot-kick for the second time in two friendlies! Here, Torriani guesses correctly, diving to his right to palm Fernandes’ strike away.

De Winter brings down Tielemans inside the box after Terracciano loses the ball attempting to play out from the back.

Manchester United 1 AC Milan 1 (Chukwueze) It’s all a bit messy. Jashari causes Maguire and Santos to crash into each other (Kaka at Old Trafford, anyone?) off a throw-in, Ramos taking over with the United pair out of commission. He finds Chukwueze who finishes the move off at the far post.

The match becomes stretched momentarily as Pavlovic, the centre-back, marauds forward, setting the ball to Estupinan who delivers another dangerous cross from the left, which Lammens does well to claim.

Santos clips Loftus-Cheek near the byline and the referee awards Milan a free-kick. Chukwueze cuts the ball back to an unmarked Jashari on the edge of the box, but his side-footed effort flies wide.

Milan supporters unfurl a banner paying tribute to the late, great Franco Baresi, who passed away on July 31 aged 66.

Hermosa bandera a Franco Baresi.QUE EN PAZ DESCANSE, LEYENDA DEL FÚTBOL 🙏🏻 pic.twitter.com/fvE48nKVSs

United have picked their moments to press. Santos, who has enjoyed a wonderful pre-season, is a little too overzealous in his attempts to regain possession and gives away a foul. But the intent is correct.

Shaw floats a delightful ball over the top for Fernandes to gallop on to. The Portuguese steals in ahead of De Winter but cannot find the target with his weaker left foot.

Cisse escapes the clutches of Mazraoui down the left and fires a shot (more likely a mis-hit cross) straight into the gloves of Lammens.

United finally get their foot on the ball, but Heaven attempts an ambitious cross-field pass and possession goes back to the Italians.

A Mexican wave has already begun. We’re only 21 minutes in...

Carrick’s side continue to sit off, allowing Milan to keep hold of the ball. Cisse works in from the left, playing a neat one-two with Ramos before his curled strike sails well over.

A period of extended possession for Milan, United dropping into a compact 4-4-2 mid-block. Estupinan rains in a dangerous cross from the left and the ball falls to Loftus-Cheek, whose effort is expertly saved by the right boot of Lammens.

Estupinan goes into the book after pulling Amad’s shirt as he looked to dart in behind after Tielemans had played a dangerous through-ball. Might possibly have been the last man?

Tielemans cedes possession to the busy Jashari just outside his own box, the Swiss midfielder moving the ball on to Loftus-Cheek who fires a shot straight at Lammens.

Amad picks Pavlovic’s pocket and the Milan centre-half is forced to concede a corner. United unable to score from this one.

Milan are indeed in Amorim’s preferred 3-4-2-1 formation. They circulate the ball in front of United’s first line of pressure in an attempt to calm things down.

Manchester United 1 AC Milan 0 (Maguire) Fernandes delivers an inswinger from the left and Maguire is there to meet it at the back post, striding past Musa to plant a header past Torriani.

United make a fast start, Dorgu flashing a cross-cum-shot across the face of goal. Torriani gets a fingertip to it and thte ball goes behind for a corner.

Szymon Marciniak, the experienced Polish referee, gets us under way. Milan send the ball back to goalkeeper Torriani.

The players emerge from the tunnel, United debuting their lovely new cream third kit and Milan in their traditional red-and-black home colours. Smoke machines and pyrotechnics add to the atmosphere in Wroclaw...

We are almost ready to go. Let us know your match predictions and thoughts on United’s prospects this season in the comments section beneath this blog.

Manchester United defeated Leeds United on penalties to hoist the mighty Boyle Sports Cup at Croke Park. The match, a 1-1 draw, was brought to an abrupt end after five young pitch invaders ran to the middle of the field to take selfies with Bruno Fernandes. In the shoot-out it was James Justin who missed the “decisive” spot-kick, paving the way for Noussair Mazraoui to win it for United.

Marcus Rashford is on the bench this afternoon and could make his first United appearance since his cameo in a Europa League win over Viktoria Plzen in December 2024. He was frozen out under Amorim and has since been loaned to Aston Villa and Barcelona, but his Old Trafford future under Carrick remains unclear.

Michael Carrick believes Manchester United can push for the Premier League title, but has underlined the urgent need for signings.

The United head coach has taken heart from his squad’s promising preparations for the new campaign and, speaking at their Co Kildare summer base, he explained why he was confident they could build on last season’s third-place finish.

Carrick has been thrilled to hear United’s players discussing what they might achieve and has dared supporters to dream that they can get closer to last year’s champions Arsenal. But he is also a realist and recognises he is not blessed with options.

So far United have added Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Karl Darlow, a reserve goalkeeper, but their £83.3m spend is significantly less than what newly promoted clubs Ipswich Town (£109.4m) and Coventry City (£92.2m) have invested in their squads.

Amorim’s side have gone intercontinental this summer, travelling from Scotland to Indonesia, via Australia, before arriving in Poland for the last of their four pre-season games.

In memory of Franco Baresi 🇮🇹♾️ pic.twitter.com/ULAJRjxDvE

Manchester United Lammens; Mazraoui, Maguire, Heaven, Shaw; Tielemans, Santos, Fernandes; Amad, Dorgu; Cunha

Subs Heath, Mee, Amass, Dalot, Martínez, Yoro, Collyer, J. Fletcher, T. Fletcher, Mainoo, Gabriel, Lacey, Mbeumo, Rashford, Zirkzee

AC Milan Torriani; Terracciano, De Winter, Pavlović; Chukwueze, Jashari, Musah, Estupiñán; Loftus-Cheek, Cissè; Ramos

Subs Bouyer, Pittarella, Gila, Diawara, Vladimirov, Ricci, Saelemaekers, Bartesaghi, Modrić, Comotto, Camarda

At his AC Milan unveiling, Amorim was asked about the learnings from his United tenure that he would take into his new role. He said: “The first thing is it’s hard to explain the mistakes because for that I would have to explain the context of the last adventure.

“It’s hard to say to you every mistake. The only thing I can say is that I learned a lot and I made some mistakes.

“I didn’t have the opportunity, and I’m sorry for that, I didn’t have the opportunity to say something to the Manchester United fans at the moment and I’m really proud to be their coach for a year in that time.

“But now it’s a different history. There are a lot of things that I could do better in the last experience but sometimes it’s like that, you need to learn to find the right spot to reach a different level and that’s my thinking here.

“Everyone learns from their experience. I learned a lot, I did some mistakes I will try to change, there are some thing you will never change but I think I will be a better manager, that’s all.”

Welcome to live coverage of Manchester United’s final pre-season match, against AC Milan in Wroclaw, Poland. Michael Carrick’s side will look to apply the finishing touches to a promising summer on the pitch, which has included victories over Rosenborg and Atlético Madrid, plus a draw against European champions Paris St-Germain. The team will fly back to Manchester with the big ones, the ones they have always wanted – the Snapdragon Cup and the Boyle Sports Cup – in tow.

At the Tarczynski Stadium there will be a reunion with former manager Ruben Amorim, who was appointed AC Milan’s head coach in June, five months after being sacked by United. Following a frustrating season under Massimiliano Allegri in which Milan fell out of the Champions League spots on the final day, the Rossoneri said Amorim would bring a “modern dominant tactical approach”. His methods failed to cut through at Old Trafford, though, during a tumultuous 14-month reign which finally ended after the Portuguese “blew up” during a heated meeting with director of football Jason Wilcox. At Milan, Amorim has persisted with the 3-4-2-1 formation that was doomed at United.

Carrick made clear this week that United must strengthen if they are to challenge for titles. So far the club have brought in Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Karl Darlow, but they are still in the market for a left-back and another midfielder. The future of Marcus Rashford has also been a topic of conversation among United fans. The forward has not played for his boyhood club since December 2024 but has joined up with his team-mates in Poland and it remains to be seen if he features in Carrick’s forward planning.

Kobbie Mainoo, who did not play a minute at this summer’s World Cup, and Lisandro Martínez have also joined up with the team this week and could be handed their first minutes of pre-season having been named in the matchday squad. For Milan, new signing Gonçalo Ramos – bought from PSG for £63m – will make his first appearance in the famous red and black.

#2070. Füllkrug Admission Raises Uncomfortable Question About West Ham’s Striker Recruitment

Ordinarily, I wouldn’t be in too much of a hurry to pay attention to what Niclas Füllkrug says about West Ham. However, the fact that he currently tops the Bundesliga goalscoring charts with nine goals in nine games for Werder Bremen does lend some credibility to his latest comments.

Speaking while on international duty with Germany, Füllkrug has suggested that a lack of service was partly responsible for his struggles at West Ham and AC Milan. In an interview published by the German Football Association, he explained that his Bremen teammates actively look to find him with the ball, something he felt was missing at his previous two clubs.

The German striker cost West Ham £27 million when he arrived from Borussia Dortmund, and there’s little doubt in my mind that the Hammers failed to have a proper plan for incorporating him into the team. However, Füllkrug must also take his share of the blame because his first season was blighted by injury, and he also spoke about feeling homesick.

The truth is that Füllkrug was never really on the pitch for long enough for us to discover whether anything could have come from his transfer. His constant fitness problems made it almost impossible to establish any consistency, and he has now acknowledged that staying fit was the key issue during his time abroad.

That said, there is little in West Ham’s performances under Julen Lopetegui, Graham Potter or Nuno Espírito Santo that suggests we would have been able to get the best out of what is clearly a talented striker.

There may well be something in his assertion that he wasn’t given a decent supply line when he did play for West Ham. Indeed, we’ve previously looked at how Bremen have built their attacking play around Füllkrug, with teammates providing the service and support he so often appeared to lack in East London.

As for his fitness, I’m afraid that’s very much on him. West Ham have consistently demonstrated over the past few years that their medical team, physiotherapists and fitness staff have generally done a good job of keeping players available.

Füllkrug’s injury record was a significant part of the problem, and whilst it’s perfectly reasonable for him to question the service he received, it doesn’t explain why he spent so much of his West Ham career unavailable for selection.

Nevertheless, watching a striker who managed just three goals for West Ham now leading the Bundesliga scoring charts is bound to raise questions about the original recruitment decision. The fact that the club are still dealing with the financial consequences of his move only adds to the frustration.

Füllkrug has rediscovered his goalscoring touch at Bremen, and good luck to him. But I suspect the truth about his West Ham failure lies somewhere between the club not knowing how to use him and the player simply not being fit enough to give himself a proper chance.

#2069. Premier League KMI panel issues emphatic verdict on Alexander Isak penalty decision v Arsenal

The Premier League’s Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel has concluded that Liverpool should’ve had a penalty awarded for an offence by Jurrien Timber on Alexander Isak in their defeat to Arsenal earlier this month.

Five minutes after Kai Havertz scored the only goal of the game at Anfield, the Swedish striker had his shirt pulled in the box by the Gunners defender, but neither on-field referee Andy Madley nor Stuart Attwell on VAR felt compelled to award a spot kick despite the transgression being clear.

The Reds’ head coach Andoni Iraola went as far as claiming that a penalty would’ve been awarded had our number 9 gone to ground instead of staying on his feet when his jersey was grabbed.

On Wednesday, the Premier League published the findings of several incidents reviewed by the KMI Panel, including the one involving Isak and Timber on 1 November.

Their verdict reads (via premierleague.com): ‘The panel felt that a penalty should have been awarded for a holding action by Timber on Isak, 4:1. One panellist considered the short-lived holding to lack clear impact on the ability of Isak to progress.

‘The majority also felt that VAR should have intervened to recommend an on-field review, 3:2, on the basis that it was a clear and obvious error. Two panellists considered that the subjectivity in assessing impact meant this did not meet the high threshold for VAR intervention.’

The KMI Panel concluded: ‘In this instance the panel deemed that Timber’s challenge on Isak met the threshold for a holding offence and should have resulted in a penalty kick, both on-field and through VAR intervention.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

How nice of the KMI Panel to come back and tell us what was so damn obvious at the time of the incident – or at least obvious to anyone not named Andy Madley or Stuart Attwell, or whichever member of the panel felt that the right decision was made on the day.

How that individual concluded that Timber’s actions lacked ‘clear impact on the ability of Isak to progress’ is baffling – the Liverpool striker would surely have gotten on the end of Bradley Barcola’s cross had his shirt not been so blatantly pulled.

The panel’s verdict today won’t come as much consolation to anyone involved with the Reds, who were deprived of a legitimate penalty which – if converted – could’ve significantly altered the course of a match that they lost 1-0.

It’s not much good being told in retrospect that the officials got it wrong; these are clear decisions that professional referees should be capable of getting correct at the time, especially when they have the fallback option of VAR.

We get that many incidents are subjective and that consensus will never be achieved when it comes to refereeing in the Premier League, but there’s simply no excuse for botching calls like the Timber/Isak incident 10 days ago.

#2068. The Premier League and The FA have now released this joint statement

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The FA and the Premier League have released a joint statement.

The official release made public on Thursday morning.

The EFL and WSL also part of this joint statement.

The official statement beginning: ‘ The Premier League, The FA, EFL and WSL Football stand with all survivors of non-recent child sexual abuse in football and acknowledge the profound and enduring impact it has on the individuals and their loved ones.’

This statement then going on to detail: ‘The FA launched Voices of Truth, an acknowledgement of survivors’ courageous disclosures, which were a landmark moment in English football. Through the collective efforts of Clubs, Leagues, The FA and County FAs, we continue to make significant progress in strengthening safeguarding measures to promote and protect the safety and welfare of children, young people and adults at risk.’

The official release then going on to detail: ‘We have further deepened the provision of education and training, and strengthened how Clubs, academies and County FAs are audited and assessed. Reporting pathways are now more effective, and there is clearer oversight and accountability across the game. The annual Play Safe campaign continues to shine a light on the robust preventative measures now in place, highlighting the importance of children and young people’s voices as part of this work and reinforcing that safeguarding is a collective responsibility.’

The statement then adding: ‘Importantly, we also know that this work is never finished; it requires ongoing vigilance, steadfast commitment and bold leadership. We will never waver in our commitment to putting the safety and wellbeing of children and young people at the very heart of our work, while continuing to ensure that support remains accessible to all those affected by abuse.’

The joint release then giving out the following: ‘Information about confidential support services can be found here, with further information also available through Voices of Truth, a new, survivor-led digital platform hosted on The FA website. Any current safeguarding concern about a child or adult at risk should be reported without delay through the appropriate safeguarding reporting channels, or directly to the police in an emergency.’

#2067. West Ham Target Giant Rangers Striker As Koppen Looks To Scotland

West Ham United have been linked with a January move for Rangers striker Ryan Naderi, although the Scottish club are reportedly reluctant to sell their 6ft 4in centre-forward. According to TEAMtalk journalist Fraser Fletcher, the Hammers and Wolves are among several clubs monitoring the 23-year-old.

Naderi has registered 14 goal contributions in 17 appearances this season, attracting interest from England and Germany. However, Rangers are understood to be wary of entertaining a January sale as they chase the Scottish Premiership title.

The link is particularly interesting given West Ham’s search for a replacement for Taty Castellanos. As Claret & Hugh exclusively revealed yesterday, Nils Koppen has already approached a France based striker ahead of the January transfer window, while the club would consider offers for the Argentine.

To see West Ham linked with a striker from Rangers should really come as no surprise.

After all, the Hammers have recruited several senior executives with connections to Ibrox, including Koppen and new chief financial officer James Taylor, who previously worked together at Rangers alongside acting chief executive Karim Virani.

Given those relationships, it stands to reason that Koppen would have a particularly close eye on developments at his former club.

In fact, it’s not just the blue half of Glasgow where Koppen appears to have his finger on the pulse. West Ham broke the Championship transfer record during the summer by bringing Arne Engels to east London from Celtic.

Koppen worked at Rangers as Director of Football

At 6ft 4in, Naderi certainly offers the physical presence of a traditional centre-forward. The German-born Czech international joined Rangers from Hansa Rostock earlier this year and has made an impressive start to life in Scottish football.

Whether he is the right striker for Scott Parker remains to be seen, but the reported interest makes sense given West Ham’s need to strengthen their attacking options.

I very much doubt this is about replacing Joël Piroe, who remains part of Parker’s plans. The more pressing issue is Castellanos, with West Ham already exploring the possibility of moving on the £27 million striker.

Given Koppen’s connections in Glasgow and West Ham’s search for another centre-forward, this is one transfer link that doesn’t require too much imagination to seem believable.

#2065. Any three of these seventeen Premier League teams could be relegated this season

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Looking at the 20 Premier League teams this season, which ones do you think will end up relegated?

I think it is a tough one, a really tough one…

We appeared to have reached a point where it was looking all but impossible for clubs to come up from the Championship and survive.

In the 2024-25 season, all three Premier League teams that had been promoted from the Championship in May 2024 were all relegated with a pitiful number of points. They only picked up 59 points in total from their 114 collective fixtures with Leicester 25 points, Ipswich 22 points and Southampton 12 points, they won only 12 Premier League matches between them.

It is early days but from a total of 30 collective attempts this season, you have Ipswich, Hull and Coventry having picked up eight wins and seven draws between them and 31 points.

One or more of them may well end up relegated but I don’t think any of that trio are guaranteed to go down this time, immediately after having escaped from the Championship.

The current Premier League table on Thursday 12 November 2026

I honestly think that it is a case of any three from the following seventeen Premier League clubs who will be relegated.

Aston Villa Bournemouth Brentford Chelsea Coventry Crystal Palace Everton Fulham Hull Ipswich Leeds Manchester City Manchester United Newcastle United Nottingham Forest Sunderland Tottenham

Apart from Arsenal, Brighton and probably Liverpool, I don’t think any of the Premier League teams are safe.

By this point after ten games of the 2025-26 Premier League season: Eight Premier League teams had 17 or more points (this season only four have 17+). There was a gap of 16 points between 5th top and 20th (this season only nine points). Twelve Premier League teams had won at least four matches (this season seven).

I am guessing that some of you are puzzled about the inclusion of Manchester City, but if/when their appeal fails against the 114 guilty verdicts on breaches of Premier League rules, every chance that relegation will be the key punishment.

Put it this way, only Hull and Coventry are seen by the bookies as more likely to be relegated than Manchester City.

Last season you needed 40 points for safety, with West Ham ending the season on 39 points in 18th place.

Plenty of people will think it is impossible for say Manchester United to be relegated, when they have such huge advantages on almost all other Premier League clubs when it comes to their ability to spend on transfer fees and wages.

If Manchester United hadn’t fluked a home win against Aston Villa on the final day of the 2024-25 season they would have finished on 39 points. Before that Villa match Man U had only won four of their last 21 EPL games and picked up 17 points. Considering they only have one win and eight points from their first ten Premier League games this 2026-27 season, what if Manchester United had a similar end to this campaign as they had two seasons ago?

The Premier League is so competitive this season, so many teams can beat each other, pretty much anything is possible…

#2064. West Ham Taty Transfer Talks Could Open Door To Goalkeeper Deal

According to a number of reports, River Plate are exploring a move for Valentín Castellanos, with an initial loan proposal understood to be one of the options being discussed. The Argentine giants are believed to be assessing whether a temporary agreement could be structured with West Ham contributing towards a portion of the forward’s wages to help make the deal financially viable.

The Argentinian side are also open to exploring a deal in which they would acquire Castellanos while West Ham retain a percentage of his future transfer rights, reducing the upfront fee required.

While the prospect of regular football in South America may appeal to the player, any negotiations are unlikely to be straightforward.

A Taty transfer to River Plate could result in Beltran moving in the opposite direction.

While West Ham are understood to be open to parting ways with Castellanos, the club would want a significantly higher transfer fee than the figures currently being considered by River Plate, creating a sizeable gap between the two clubs’ positions.

Our trusted transfer source suggests it’s unlikely that the Argentinians can afford the striker, as teams over there don’t have any money, yet reaffirmed the striker is very much up for sale.

From West Ham’s perspective, agreeing to subsidise wages while also accepting a heavily discounted transfer fee makes little financial sense unless there are performance-related add-ons or future sell-on clauses that could bridge the gap.

The situation remains at an early stage and there is no indication that a breakthrough is imminent. However, River Plate’s interest appears genuine, and negotiations could continue if the Argentine club can move closer to West Ham’s expectations.

There are also suggestions that Santiago Beltrán, as reported by Gonzo yesterday, is of interest to West Ham, which opens up the possibility of the goalkeeper being included in any deal.

For now, the ball is firmly in River Plate’s court. If they want to bring Castellanos back to South American football, a significantly improved proposal will be required before West Ham consider doing business.

#2062. West Ham’s Leadership Problem Goes Far Beyond Championship Experience

West Ham’s lack of Championship experience has been highlighted by former striker Sam Parkin, who believes the Hammers are missing the know-how required to negotiate difficult away matches.

Speaking on the Sky Sports EFL Show, Parkin questioned whether West Ham have enough experienced organisers in the team, with The72 highlighting his concerns about a midfield containing Arne Engels, Mohamadou Kanté and Divine Mukasa.

Let’s be absolutely clear about this. West Ham lack leaders, full stop. I believe this is partly a consequence of Graham Potter’s clear-out, something highlighted in Michail Antonio’s book, with the former manager appearing to move on some of the bigger personalities at the club. And let’s be fair, they’ve not really been replaced.

However, I think there are two separate issues here. One is leadership, while the other is tactical nous, and I’m not convinced they’re necessarily solved by the same player.

If West Ham are looking for somebody prepared to scrap, they really need look no further than Edson Álvarez. The Mexican is already at the club despite having been frozen out under Nuno Espírito Santo, and he would immediately bring some bite to the midfield.

From a tactical point of view, I suspect Scott Parker will persevere with Soungoutou Magassa in defensive midfield once he gets back up to full fitness. Parker has already brought him back into the picture, and a specialist defensive midfielder could make a significant difference to how West Ham cope when games become physical or untidy.

Longer term, though, there is little doubt West Ham should be looking at the personalities they’re recruiting, not simply the technical ability of individual players.

When Director of Player Recruitment Nils Koppen assesses potential January signings, I’d like to think he’ll be considering whether they can organise those around them, take responsibility and provide leadership when things aren’t going well.

Parkin makes a fair point about Championship experience, but for me the issue goes deeper than knowing the division. West Ham have lost too many big personalities without replacing them, and that’s something Parker and Koppen will eventually have to address.

#2060. West Ham Linked With Swansea Star As Magassa Exit Rumours Emerge

West Ham United have been linked with a January move for Swansea City midfielder Marko Stamenić, although I must admit I’m struggling to see why another central midfielder would be a priority for the Hammers.

According to Keith Haynes of Swansea Independent, both West Ham and Southampton are monitoring the 24-year-old New Zealand international. The report suggests Stamenić’s passing ability and defensive awareness have attracted attention, although no formal approach has been confirmed.

West Ham supporters might remember the midfielder from our 1-0 victory over Swansea in October. Stamenić was dispossessed by Divine Mukasa in the build-up to the winning goal, with the young Hammer eventually finishing the move himself. However, that particular incident is hardly a reason to judge a player’s overall ability.

Personally, I think the last thing West Ham need at the moment is another central midfielder. I can think of at least four positions that require strengthening before we start looking to add more players in that department.

We’ve already got Arne Engels, Divine Mukasa, Mohamadou Kanté, Lewis Orford, Tomáš Souček and Soungoutou Magassa, among others. Indeed, the number of midfield options available has been a talking point throughout the season.

More interestingly, the Swansea report also suggests that Magassa could leave West Ham in January, although that remains unconfirmed.

West Ham paid Monaco approximately £20 million for Magassa, but his lack of involvement under Nuno Espírito Santo has hardly helped maintain his transfer value. I would suggest that his valuation has depreciated significantly since arriving at the club.

Given that Scott Parker immediately brought Magassa back into his starting line-up against Cardiff, there is at least some indication that the new manager sees a role for that type of defensive midfielder.

Scott Parker scouted Magassa during his time at Monaco

For me, the sensible approach would be to get Magassa involved in the first team, build up his match fitness and see whether Parker can coax the performances out of him that persuaded West Ham to spend £20 million in the first place.

That would give us a better player and potentially restore some of his transfer value, rather than selling him at what could be a considerable loss.

Stamenić may well be a decent enough footballer, and his reported statistics at Swansea are encouraging. But unless there is a significant departure from West Ham’s midfield, I really don’t see the logic in spending more money on a position where we already have plenty of options.

Surely there are more pressing problems for Nils Koppen to solve in January.

#2059. West Ham Fanzine Blowing Bubbles Shortlisted for National Award

West Ham might be lumbering in mid-table but Hammers fanzine Blowing Bubbles is very much top of class after it was shortlisted for Fanzine of the Year at the 2026 Football Supporters’ Association Awards.

It’s the fourth time the publication has received the recognition, having previously been nominated in 2015, 2021 and 2023. Blowing Bubbles joins five other finalists, including Sunderland’s A Love Supreme, Leeds United’s The Square Ball and Middlesbrough’s Fly Me To The Moon.

Editor David Blackmore launched Blowing Bubbles in the summer of 2012 and has been involved ever since. The publication celebrated its 100th edition in February 2020 and has now reached issue 173, which is quite an achievement for an independent monthly football fanzine.

“I’m absolutely delighted that Blowing Bubbles has been shortlisted for Fanzine of the Year for a fourth time. To be in such an elite group of fantastic football publications is a massive pat on the back and recognition of not only the huge amount of time and effort we put into producing every issue but also to the continued support we’ve had from the West Ham Family.”

Anyone involved in producing independent football content will appreciate the work that goes into keeping a publication going month after month. Credit must also go to David’s team of writers and designer Kelvin Farrell.

The winners will be announced on Monday 30 November at London’s Nobu, Portman Square, with Victoria Derbyshire hosting the FSA Awards. The fanzine category will be decided by a judging panel.

From all of us at Claret & Hugh, congratulations to David and the entire Blowing Bubbles team. Best of luck on awards night. Fingers crossed you bring the trophy home!

#2058. West Ham’s £5m Winger Has Gone From Match-Winner To Liability

Whilst most concentrated on Mads Hermansen’s inability to make saves during West Ham’s 2-1 defeat to Blackburn Rovers, it allowed somebody else to escape the glare of criticism. That player was Manor Solomon, because, to put it frankly, he was awful when coming on as a substitute to replace Edvin Austbø at Ewood Park.

The Israeli international has been shocking for West Ham recently, ironically since the last round of international fixtures in September and October, when he represented his country four times and returned to East London looking completely knackered. His performances have deteriorated to the point where I struggle to see what he’s currently offering the team.

We now find ourselves in the rather strange situation where, with West Ham entering another international break, we’re hoping Solomon can go away with Israel and somehow regain some form. Because as things stand, he is simply not a viable option in the current West Ham team.

No doubt West Ham manager Scott Parker, being something of a Championship expert, would have had reasonably positive opinions of Solomon, having witnessed him tearing up the division for Leeds United during their promotion season. However, he’ll have been left in no illusion that the version of Solomon he’s inherited since replacing Nuno Espírito Santo is a long way from that player.

Solomon stunk the place out in the first half against Cardiff City before being substituted, and when introduced in place of Austbø against Blackburn, he made the team noticeably worse. It’s particularly frustrating because Austbø had looked lively and dangerous, offering the directness and attacking intent that Solomon currently seems unable to provide.

Nuno Espírito Santo pushed hard for the signing of Manor Solomon

It’s important to remember that, whilst West Ham haven’t spent a fortune bringing him in, Solomon was signed for a reported £5 million precisely because he was supposed to guarantee goals and assists in a Championship team. Unfortunately, that looks a long way off at present, and the attacking contribution we expected simply hasn’t materialised consistently enough.

Solomon has been called up by Israel for two UEFA Nations League fixtures during the November international break. He will face Kosovo away on Saturday 14 November before Israel take on Austria in Debrecen, Hungary, on Tuesday 17 November.

The winger also featured in all four of Israel’s September and October Nations League matches, so another spell of international football is hardly guaranteed to leave him refreshed. Nevertheless, West Ham and Scott Parker will be hoping those two games can kick-start Solomon into something approaching his previous form.

There is clearly a talented Championship player in there, as he demonstrated during his time at Leeds. But the player who was supposed to provide West Ham with goals, assists and attacking quality is currently struggling to make any meaningful impact.

Parker has the international break to work with much of his squad, but Solomon will be away with Israel rather than spending that time on the training pitch with his new manager. Perhaps a change of environment and a couple of international appearances will do him some good, because West Ham desperately need the Manor Solomon who helped Leeds win promotion, not the one we’ve been watching recently.

#2056. West Ham Youngsters Send Parker Message With Juventus Victory

West Ham United’s Under-21s produced an impressive performance to beat Juventus Next Gen 3-1 at Victoria Road last night, with three different players getting on the scoresheet in the Premier League International Cup.

Harry Montague, Tyrone Omotoye and Jethro Medine scored for the Hammers, who recovered from conceding an equaliser just before half-time to claim their second victory in three matches in the competition. The result moves Mark Robson’s side up to third in Group A with six points.

However, perhaps the most interesting aspect of the evening came from Robson’s comments afterwards. With Scott Parker now in charge of the West Ham first team, the academy coach made it clear that he hoped some of his youngsters had caught the attention of the senior coaching staff.

According to the official West Ham match report, the Hammers dominated much of the opening half and took the lead in the 29th minute.

Preston Fearon delivered a dangerous free-kick into the penalty area, where Montague was on hand to finish from close range.

Juventus equalised through Marco Tiozzo in the 43rd minute, but West Ham continued to create opportunities after the break.

Omotoye restored the lead in the 58th minute, finishing clinically from Jephthah Medine’s cross, before Jethro Medine converted a stoppage-time penalty to complete a thoroughly deserved victory.

Robson was particularly pleased with the contribution of several younger players who had stepped up from the Under-18s.

Speaking to the club’s official website, Robson said:

“We were miles better on the ball than we have been in recent games. I was really pleased with the performance.”

The former West Ham midfielder also highlighted the increased energy and aggression his side displayed compared with their previous defeat against Monaco.

However, it was his final observation that stood out.

“Hopefully, one or two of the lads impressed the first team staff that might have been here this evening.”

It’s an interesting comment given the recent managerial change at West Ham.

As Claret & Hugh recently reported, Robson returned to his Under-21 coaching role during the summer after previously working with the senior squad.

That experience should put him in a good position to judge which youngsters might eventually be capable of making the step up.

There have already been encouraging signs from young players in the first team this season, and Parker will undoubtedly be keen to assess the talent available throughout the club.

Of course, performing well against Juventus Next Gen is very different from playing Championship football. Nevertheless, the academy continues to provide reasons for optimism.

The result also follows another impressive European performance against Valencia earlier in the competition.

West Ham’s next International Cup fixture is against Jong Genk in December, while Robson’s side return to domestic cup action against Brighton Under-21s on 23 November.

#2055. ‘Right now…’ – Liverpool-linked Premier League star makes his plans clear amid transfer rumours

One Premier League player who’s reportedly being targeted by Liverpool has issued a reponse to the transfer speculation surrounding him.

Earlier this week, TEAMtalk claimed that Anfield chiefs are eyeing Bart Verbruggen as a potential long-term successor to Alisson Becker, who’s now 34 and – as it stands – will be out of contract in seven months’ time.

The Brighton goalkeeper was reportedly among a shortlist of candidates being considered by the Reds prior to the summer transfer window, with the Merseysiders eventually agreeing a deal to sign Lucca Brughmans, who’ll join from Genk next summer.

Verbruggen – who’s currently with the Netherlands squad for their concluding UEFA Nations League fixtures – has insisted that despite the rumoured interest from Liverpool, he’s more than happy with the Seagulls, who currently sit second in the Premier League.

The 24-year-old said (via NOS): “Right now we’re doing really well at Brighton, so it would be a real shame to ruin that by living in the future. I really try to stay in the moment, to focus on what is currently going on. I enjoy that, and that is also how I perform best.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Brighton’s magnificent season so far has been underpinned by the excellence of the man between the sticks, who’s kept seven clean sheets in 10 league games and conceded just three times in eight top-flight matches since a 4-3 defeat at Chelsea in August (Transfermarkt).

Figures from Fotmob show that he’s prevented 4.39 xG worth of goals for his team, more than anyone else in the Premier League, and he put in a heroic display in the Seagulls’ recent win at Manchester City as he recorded no fewer than seven saves (Sky Sports).

Those performance levels would indicate that he’d be an ideal successor to Alisson, although there’s been renewed hope in recent days that Liverpool’s number 1 could extend his contract for another year or two, with his agent currently in talks with the club to that effect.

Giorgi Mamardashvili was signed with the intention of succeeding the Brazilian eventually, although the 26-year-old hasn’t always convinced during his time with the Reds so far, and Brughmans will add to the queue once he joins ahead of next season.

Right now there wouldn’t seem to be any urgent need for LFC to move heaven and earth to sign Verbruggen, but if circumstances were to change regarding their current goalkeeping options, it could be worth keeping a hand in should the opportunity arise to move for the Brighton stopper.

#2054. West Ham Face Solomon Fitness Scare Ahead Of Preston

West Ham United winger Manor Solomon is struggling with back pain while on international duty with Israel, raising fresh concerns about his fitness ahead of the Hammers’ Championship clash with Preston North End.

According to Israeli publication Walla Sport, Solomon was only able to complete part of Wednesday’s training session ahead of Saturday’s Nations League match against Kosovo. The winger participated in the opening stages before withdrawing from the remainder of the session.

A further report on Thursday morning suggested that Solomon remained a doubt for the fixture, with his fitness due to be assessed again. There has been no confirmed withdrawal from the Israel squad, but given his recent problems, this is hardly the news West Ham supporters will have wanted to hear.

I am fully aware I might be contradicting myself here, having previously wanted Solomon to play for his country as a way of kick-starting his West Ham form. But this injury concern does cast the situation in a completely new light.

I understand that the left winger is an important player for Israel, but as I’ve made the case repeatedly, I believe his poor form is a direct result of him being overplayed by his country during the last international break.

Indeed, Claret & Hugh reported Solomon’s back problems during the October international break, when a club source confirmed that the winger was suffering considerable pain.

And if he is injured, or even feeling some pain in training, there is no way he should be risked against Kosovo.

There is simply too much at stake for West Ham to have a player returning from international duty in a worse physical condition than when he left.

That said, I do think Edvin Austbø has moved ahead of Solomon in the pecking order to start against Preston on West Ham’s left wing.

Solomon has struggled to find his best form, while Austbø has been pushing hard for an opportunity to impress new gaffer Scott Parker. Even if both players return fully fit, I would be inclined to give the Norwegian the starting place.

There is no suggestion at this stage that Solomon will miss the Preston match, and hopefully this turns out to be nothing more than a precaution.

However, given what happened during the previous international break, surely the sensible thing is to avoid taking any unnecessary risks.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Fabian Hurzeler's men are five points adrift of leaders Arsenal and one ahead of third placed Manchester City.

"There is an argument to be made that they would be the nearest pursuers to Arsenal," said Goodman, speaking to Betway.

"For Brighton to be able to sustain it through a 38-game Premier League season and a European campaign, you kind of think maybe not win the league, but absolutely, you hope that they can be challenging for a top-four Champions League spot."

Goodman, who had a prolific career as a striker for the likes of West Bromwich Albion, Sunderland and Wolves, has been impressed by the rise of Brighton and believes it’s just reward for how the club operates and long-term planning.

“I’ve been commentating for Sky Sports for 20 years next March, and I’ve commentated on Brighton and Hove Albion in League One and a lot in the Championship over that period of time,” Goodman added.

#2052. Scott Parker Has Two Weeks To Solve West Ham’s Pressing Problem

West Ham have been given a fairly clear indication of what to expect from Preston North End when the two sides meet after the international break. Preston manager Graham Alexander has been explaining the aggressive pressing approach that helped his team beat Southampton, and it’s something Scott Parker will undoubtedly need to consider.

Speaking to the Lancashire Evening Post following the victory, Alexander said: “We pressed everything.” Preston outshot Southampton 12-3 in the first half, and their manager intends to use the break to reinforce that approach.

Without wishing to belittle Preston’s performance against Southampton, I have to say West Ham are in big trouble if we can’t beat them, irrespective of what their press might be. We can analyse the opposition’s tactics until we’re blue in the face, but ultimately West Ham should have enough quality to overcome Preston.

Parker has two weeks on the training ground to drill his players, and I would expect that time to be significant. He’s barely had an opportunity to work properly with the squad since replacing Nuno Espírito Santo, something that was evident during the defeat at Blackburn Rovers.

Parker has a philosophy of wanting to keep the ball, so I suspect he’ll want West Ham to play their way through Preston’s press rather than simply bypassing it with long balls. Of course, that requires players who are comfortable receiving possession under pressure and know where their next pass is going.

I also believe we’ll see a specialist defensive midfielder, such as Soungoutou Magassa, used more often than not for the remainder of the season. Parker has already shown a willingness to use Magassa, and having somebody in that position could prove particularly important when opponents attempt to press West Ham high up the pitch.

Preston’s victory over Southampton was a decent result, but it doesn’t suddenly make them an opponent West Ham should fear. Quite frankly, if the Hammers can’t beat the likes of Preston in our own backyard we don’t deserve to get promoted.

Parker has been given a valuable fortnight to work on his methods, and the expectation has to be that we return from the international break looking considerably better organised.

Whether Preston press high, sit deep or alternate between the two, West Ham need to be capable of dealing with it. That’s the challenge facing Parker, and I don’t think it’s an unreasonable expectation.

#2051. West Ham’s Interest In Sydie Peck Resurfaces After Summer Pursuit

West Ham United have once again been linked with Sheffield United midfielder Sydie Peck, with transfer journalist Ekrem Konur reporting that the Hammers are continuing to scout the 22-year-old.

The England Under-21 international has attracted attention from several clubs, with Newcastle United and Sunderland also named in the report. Peck has certainly done his reputation no harm recently, scoring a hat-trick against Preston North End earlier this month, although there is no suggestion that West Ham have made a formal approach.

Interestingly, this isn’t the first time Peck has been linked with a move to the London Stadium. ExWHUEmployee reported through The West Ham Way back in July that West Ham had been monitoring the midfielder even before the arrival of director of recruitment Nils Koppen.

I looked quite closely at Peck during the summer when West Ham were first linked with him, and I have to say, he was a player who caught the attention.

Back then, however, we didn’t know who was staying and who was going, and the midfield situation was very different.

Since then, West Ham have signed Arne Engels and retained Soungoutou Magassa, while Mohamadou Kanté has emerged as one of the most encouraging performers of the season.

I think Peck is a decent player. Very good, in fact, and somebody who would be extremely useful in the Championship.

But unless there are due to be significant outgoings, I just cannot see this one happening.

Kante has become an important player for West Ham

Lewis Orford is not getting enough game time as it is, and Mohamadou Kanté is having one hell of a breakout season. I wouldn’t particularly want to bring anybody in who might stop that.

And let’s not forget the point Nils Koppen has made about West Ham’s recruitment strategy: the club don’t want to sign players who block the pathway of youngsters coming through.

It’s a philosophy I agree with, particularly when we’ve got young players already showing that they deserve opportunities.

There is clearly something about Peck that West Ham’s recruitment department likes. After all, the interest was being reported before Koppen arrived, and his performances for Sheffield United have only strengthened his case.

But there’s a difference between identifying a good player and identifying a player you actually need.

West Ham have more pressing areas of the squad to strengthen, and unless Scott Parker is expecting a major shake-up in midfield, I’d be surprised to see the club pursue this particular deal in January.
